add_subtopics.title: Schema migrations: changing a live schema safely
add_subtopics.body:
A schema is never finished. Six weeks into a pilot the customer wants a country column, a renamed field or a new table. On a live database you cannot just edit the CREATE TABLE file, because the tables already exist and hold data. Instead you write a migration: a small, numbered script that moves the schema from one version to the next, kept in git next to the app code. A tool records which migrations have run in a table inside the database, so every environment (your laptop, staging, production) is upgraded the same way.

For Python and SQLAlchemy the usual tool is Alembic. Flyway and Liquibase are common in Java shops, and dbt handles warehouse models separately (see warehouse). The everyday Alembic commands are: alembic revision -m "add country" (create a new file; add --autogenerate to draft it from your SQLAlchemy models, then always read it), alembic upgrade head (apply everything not yet run), alembic downgrade -1 (undo the last one) and alembic current (show the version).

During a rolling deploy the old and new app versions run at the same time for a few minutes, so every migration must work with both. That leads to expand and contract. To rename a column: expand by adding the new column and writing to both, backfill old rows, switch reads to the new column, and only in a later release contract by dropping the old one. Never rename or drop in the same release that stops using a column.

Adding a required column follows the same idea. In PostgreSQL 11 and later, ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT 'GB' with a constant default is instant. When the value must be computed per row, add the column as nullable, backfill in batches, then set NOT NULL.
add_subtopics.example: Brightside expands into Ireland and needs a country on every customer. The FDE writes migration 0007 below. In staging it adds the column, backfills 41,200 existing customers with 'GB' and then makes the column required. The old app version, which never mentions country, keeps inserting customers during the deploy and those rows get 'GB' from the server default. Later the team renames city to town with expand and contract across two releases: release 1 adds town and writes both, a backfill copies city into town, release 2 reads town, and release 3 drops city.
add_subtopics.code:
"""add country to customers

Revision ID: 0007_add_country
Revises: 0006_add_tags
"""
from alembic import op
import sqlalchemy as sa

revision = "0007_add_country"
down_revision = "0006_add_tags"


def upgrade():
    # 1. Expand: add the column as nullable, so old app code keeps working
    op.add_column("customers", sa.Column("country", sa.Text(), nullable=True))
    # 2. Backfill existing rows (in batches of about 10,000 on a big table)
    op.execute("UPDATE customers SET country = 'GB' WHERE country IS NULL")
    # 3. Only now make it required, with a default for new rows
    op.alter_column("customers", "country", nullable=False, server_default="GB")


def downgrade():
    op.drop_column("customers", "country")
checklist: Migration file is in git and reviewed like code
Autogenerated migrations were read line by line
Works with both the old and the new app version
Large backfills run in batches, not one giant UPDATE
Tested upgrade and downgrade on a copy of production data
Backup or snapshot taken before running in production

replace_subtopics.title: Tables, primary keys and foreign keys
replace_subtopics.body:
A relational database stores data in tables. Each table should describe one kind of thing: customers, products, orders. Each row is one instance of that thing, and each column is one attribute of it.

The primary key is how you refer to a single row. It must be unique and never empty. Many teams use a surrogate key, a meaningless number the database generates, because natural values like email addresses or names can change. You can still enforce that email is unique with a separate UNIQUE constraint.

A foreign key is a column that holds a primary key from another table. It is a promise the database checks for you: you cannot insert an order for customer 99 if customer 99 does not exist, and you cannot delete a customer who still has orders unless you say what should happen to them.

How the key is generated. Older tutorials write customer_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY. It still works, but for new tables PostgreSQL recommends the SQL-standard form customer_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY (use BIGINT if the table could pass about 2 billion rows). An identity column cannot be overwritten by accident, and its permissions and copying behave more predictably than SERIAL.

Choosing column types. Use NUMERIC(12,2) for money, never FLOAT, because floats cannot store 0.1 exactly and totals drift by fractions of a cent. Use TIMESTAMPTZ (timestamp with time zone) for moments in time: it stores an exact instant and converts to the reader's zone, while plain TIMESTAMP silently forgets which zone a value came from. In PostgreSQL, TEXT and VARCHAR(n) perform the same; use VARCHAR(n) only when a real length rule exists, such as a 2-letter country code. Use BOOLEAN for yes/no flags, not 'Y'/'N' strings. JSONB is fine for a few rare, loosely shaped extras, but anything you filter or join on deserves a real column. Most tables also get audit columns created_at and updated_at, and some use soft delete: a deleted_at column that is NULL for live rows, so a 'deleted' record can be restored and old reports still add up.

What happens on delete. A foreign key must say what happens when the parent row is deleted. The table below compares the three common choices.

Reading ER diagrams. Customers often hand you an entity-relationship (ER) diagram, and you should hand one back with your design. Each box is a table with its columns, and each line is a foreign key. In crow's-foot notation, a single bar at one end means 'exactly one', and the three-pronged crow's foot means 'many'. So a line with a bar at customers and a crow's foot at orders reads 'one customer has many orders'. Tools such as dbdiagram.io, or Mermaid's erDiagram text format, let you keep the diagram as text next to your SQL.
replace_subtopics.example:
Brightside Home, a homeware retailer, has customers and orders. The customers table has customer_id 1 for Ana Patel in Leeds. The orders table has order 5001 with customer_id = 1. If someone tries to insert order 5002 with customer_id = 77 and no customer 77 exists, PostgreSQL rejects the insert with a foreign key violation. The bad row never reaches the dashboard. The same design as a Mermaid ER diagram, which renders in GitHub, GitLab and most wikis:
erDiagram
  CUSTOMERS ||--o{ ORDERS : places
  ORDERS ||--|{ ORDER_LINES : contains
  PRODUCTS ||--o{ ORDER_LINES : "sold as"
Read ||--o{ as 'exactly one on the left, zero or more on the right'. When Ana asks to close her account, the RESTRICT rule stops a hard delete while she has orders, so Brightside sets deleted_at instead and her past orders still count in last year's revenue.

-- one table per kind of thing
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, -- surrogate key
  email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,      -- natural value, still unique
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  city        TEXT,
  is_active   BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  extras      JSONB,                     -- rare, loosely shaped fields
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),  -- audit columns
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at  TIMESTAMPTZ                -- soft delete: NULL means live
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT NOT NULL
              REFERENCES customers (customer_id)  -- foreign key
              ON DELETE RESTRICT,                 -- block orphaning
  order_date  DATE NOT NULL,
  total       NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0    -- money: never float
);

INSERT INTO customers (email, name, city)
VALUES ('ana@example.com', 'Ana Patel', 'Leeds');   -- gets id 1
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5001, 1, '2026-09-01');   -- ok
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5002, 77, '2026-09-02');  -- fails: no customer 77
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1;         -- fails: RESTRICT
-- why money is NUMERIC, not float
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 AS float_sum,       -- 0.30000000000000004
       0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric AS numeric_sum;   -- 0.3

replace_subtopics.title: 2NF and 3NF: one fact, one place
replace_subtopics.body:
A functional dependency means one column determines another. If you know the sku, you know the product name. If you know the order_id, you know the order date.

Second normal form (2NF) applies when the key has more than one column. Every non-key column must depend on the whole key. In the 1NF table the key is (order_id, sku), but product_name depends only on sku, and order_date depends only on order_id. Those are partial dependencies, so product columns move to a products table and order columns move to an orders table. What stays in order_lines is what truly needs both: the quantity, and the price charged on that line.

Third normal form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies: a non-key column that depends on another non-key column. In the orders table, name and city depend on the customer's email, and email depends on order_id. That chain means Ana's city is still copied onto every order, so customer columns move to a customers table and orders keep only customer_id. A common summary is that every non-key column should depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

Two relationship patterns come up in every design. The first is many-to-many. One order contains many products and one product appears on many orders, so neither table can hold a single foreign key to the other. The fix is a junction table (also called a bridge or link table) with one foreign key to each side and a composite primary key over both. order_lines is exactly this pattern, with extra facts (qty, unit_price) that belong to the pair. A plainer case is product tags: product_tags(sku, tag_id) with nothing else in it.

The second is one-to-one: each row in one table matches at most one row in another. You use it to split rarely used or sensitive columns away from a busy table, such as care instructions or a customer's tax details. The child table's primary key is also its foreign key to the parent, which the database uses to guarantee 'at most one'.
replace_subtopics.example: Before 3NF, Ana moves from Leeds to York. Her 38 past orders all carry 'Leeds', and an analyst updates 30 of them. Revenue by city is now split across two cities for one customer. After 3NF, city lives in one customers row and the change is a single UPDATE. Note the price: the products table keeps the current list price (6.50 for the mug), while order_lines keeps unit_price as charged. If the mug goes to 7.00 next month, past orders still show 6.50. That is correct, because the price paid is a fact about the sale. Later Brightside adds tags such as 'kitchen' and 'gift'. The mug has two tags and 'kitchen' covers both products, so the tags go in a product_tags junction table rather than a comma-separated cell, which would break 1NF again.

add_glossary: Migration
A versioned script, kept in git, that changes a live database schema from one version to the next.
Alembic
The standard schema migration tool for Python projects that use SQLAlchemy.
Expand and contract
Changing a schema in safe steps: add the new shape, move data and code over, then remove the old shape in a later release.
Junction table
A table with a foreign key to each of two tables, used to store a many-to-many relationship.
Identity column
A column whose values the database generates, written GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY; the modern replacement for SERIAL.
Soft delete
Marking a row as deleted with a deleted_at timestamp instead of removing it.
ER diagram
An entity-relationship diagram: boxes for tables and lines for the foreign keys between them.

add_subtopics.title: Deadlocks and lock ordering
add_subtopics.body:
A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other one needs. Transaction 1 locks the WH-A row and then wants STORE-14. At the same moment transaction 2 has locked STORE-14 and wants WH-A. Neither can continue, forever. PostgreSQL checks for this after waiting deadlock_timeout (1 second by default), picks one transaction as the victim and aborts it with ERROR: deadlock detected, SQLSTATE 40P01. The other transaction then finishes normally.

A deadlock is not data corruption, but it is a failed request, and under load it can become frequent. The main fix is to always lock rows in the same order everywhere in the code, for example sorted by primary key. You can take all the locks up front with SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE, then do the updates. Two transfers in opposite directions then queue behind each other instead of crossing.

Two timeouts keep waits bounded. lock_timeout makes a statement give up if it cannot get a lock within, say, 2 seconds (error 55P03, lock not available). statement_timeout cancels any statement that runs too long. Set them with SET LOCAL inside the transaction, or per role for an app user.

Finally, treat 40P01, 55P03 and serialization failures (40001) as retryable: roll back, wait a moment and rerun the whole transaction a few times. Keep transactions short so the window for a deadlock stays small.
add_subtopics.example: The pharmacy runs two stock moves at the same time: 5 units from WH-A to STORE-14 and 5 units from STORE-14 to WH-A. With move_bad each locks its source row first, and PostgreSQL aborts one with 40P01 after about a second. With move_safe both lock the two rows in sorted order, so the second simply waits half a second for the first, and both succeed. The code below reproduces both cases on a real database.
add_subtopics.code:
import threading, time
import psycopg
from psycopg import errors

DSN = "postgresql://app@localhost/sandbox"

def move_bad(src, dst, qty):
    # Locks rows in the order the caller passes them: can deadlock
    with psycopg.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - %s WHERE location = %s", (qty, src))
        time.sleep(0.5)                    # widen the window, like a slow step
        conn.execute("UPDATE stock SET qty = qty + %s WHERE location = %s", (qty, dst))

def move_safe(src, dst, qty, attempts=3):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            with psycopg.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.transaction():
                conn.execute("SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s'")   # never wait forever
                # 1. Lock both rows in ONE fixed order (sorted by location)
                conn.execute("SELECT location FROM stock WHERE location = ANY(%s) "
                             "ORDER BY location FOR UPDATE", ([src, dst],))
                # 2. Now the updates cannot deadlock with another move_safe
                conn.execute("UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - %s WHERE location = %s", (qty, src))
                time.sleep(0.5)
                conn.execute("UPDATE stock SET qty = qty + %s WHERE location = %s", (qty, dst))
            return "ok"
        except (errors.DeadlockDetected, errors.LockNotAvailable):
            time.sleep(0.1 * (attempt + 1))   # short backoff, then retry
    return "gave up"

def race(fn):
    out = []
    t1 = threading.Thread(target=lambda: out.append(safe(fn, "WH-A", "STORE-14")))
    t2 = threading.Thread(target=lambda: out.append(safe(fn, "STORE-14", "WH-A")))
    t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join()
    return sorted(out)

def safe(fn, a, b):
    try:
        return fn(a, b, 5) or "ok"
    except errors.DeadlockDetected as e:
        return f"{e.sqlstate} deadlock detected"

with psycopg.connect(DSN, autocommit=True) as conn:
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stock")    # throwaway sandbox database
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE stock (location text PRIMARY KEY, qty int)")
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('WH-A', 100), ('STORE-14', 100)")

print(race(move_bad))    # ['40P01 deadlock detected', 'ok']
print(race(move_safe))   # ['ok', 'ok']

add_subtopics.title: Transactions that span an external call
add_subtopics.body:
A database transaction can only roll back database changes. It cannot unsend an email, reverse a payment API call or un-create a ticket in the customer's CRM. This matters a lot when an AI agent approves a refund and then calls a payment service. If you call the API inside the transaction and the commit then fails, money has left but the database says 'pending'. If you commit first and then crash before the call, the database says 'approved' but no money moved.

The transactional outbox pattern fixes this. In one local transaction you update your own tables and insert a row into an outbox table describing the external action. A separate worker reads unsent outbox rows, calls the external API and marks each row sent. The action is guaranteed to be attempted if and only if the business change committed.

The worker may crash after the API call but before marking the row, so the same action can be sent twice. That is why each outbox row carries an idempotency key, a unique id the external API uses to ignore repeats (see resilient).

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED turns a table into a simple job queue: each worker locks a few unsent rows and skips rows another worker already holds, so several workers never send the same row at once.

When a business process spans several services and a later step fails, you cannot roll back the earlier ones. Instead you run compensating actions, such as issuing a refund reversal. A chain of steps with compensations is called a saga.
add_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims agent approves refund 501 for 450.00. approve_refund commits the status change and an outbox row together. Seconds later the worker sends the payout with the row's idempotency key and marks it sent. In testing, the team kills the worker right after the API call. On restart it sends the same row again, the payment API sees the same key and ignores it, and the customer is paid exactly once.
add_subtopics.code:
import json, uuid
import psycopg

DSN = "postgresql://app@localhost/sandbox"

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE refunds (refund_id bigint PRIMARY KEY, status text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id              bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  kind            text  NOT NULL,
  payload         jsonb NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key uuid  NOT NULL UNIQUE,   -- sent to the payment API
  sent_at         timestamptz              -- NULL = still to send
);"""

def approve_refund(conn, refund_id, amount):
    # ONE local transaction: the status change and the "send money"
    # request are committed together or not at all. No API call here.
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("UPDATE refunds SET status = 'approved' WHERE refund_id = %s",
                     (refund_id,))
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO outbox (kind, payload, idempotency_key) "
                     "VALUES ('payout', %s, %s)",
                     (json.dumps({"refund_id": refund_id, "amount": amount}),
                      uuid.uuid4()))

def send_pending(conn, pay_api, batch=10):
    # Worker: SKIP LOCKED lets several workers share the queue safely
    with conn.transaction():
        rows = conn.execute("""
            SELECT id, payload, idempotency_key FROM outbox
             WHERE sent_at IS NULL
             ORDER BY id
             LIMIT %s
             FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED""", (batch,)).fetchall()
        for row_id, payload, key in rows:
            # If we crash after this call but before COMMIT, the row is sent
            # again next time. The idempotency key makes the API ignore the repeat.
            pay_api(payload, idempotency_key=str(key))
            conn.execute("UPDATE outbox SET sent_at = now() WHERE id = %s", (row_id,))
    return len(rows)

with psycopg.connect(DSN, autocommit=True) as conn:
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS refunds, outbox")
    conn.execute(SCHEMA)
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO refunds VALUES (501, 'pending')")
    approve_refund(conn, 501, 450.00)
    seen = set()
    def fake_pay_api(payload, idempotency_key):
        if idempotency_key in seen:
            return "duplicate ignored"
        seen.add(idempotency_key)
        print("paid", payload["amount"], "for refund", payload["refund_id"])
    print(send_pending(conn, fake_pay_api))   # paid 450.0 for refund 501, then 1
    print(send_pending(conn, fake_pay_api))   # 0: nothing left to send

replace_subtopics.title: Atomicity: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
replace_subtopics.body:
You start a transaction with BEGIN. Every statement after it is part of the same unit until COMMIT, which makes the changes permanent, or ROLLBACK, which undoes them.

If any statement fails, the database will not let you commit a partial result. In PostgreSQL, the transaction enters an aborted state and you must roll back.

In application code, most libraries give you a context manager or 'with' block that commits on success and rolls back on any exception. Use it, so you never forget to close a transaction.

Savepoints give you a transaction inside a transaction. SAVEPOINT marks a point, and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work after it, while the outer transaction carries on. In psycopg 3 you get one automatically by nesting conn.transaction() blocks: the outer block runs BEGIN and COMMIT, each inner block runs SAVEPOINT and, on error, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT. This is how you skip one bad row in an import without losing the good ones.

Many apps do not write SQL by hand but use an ORM (object-relational mapper) such as SQLAlchemy. There the transaction is the session: with session.begin(): commits when the block ends and rolls back if an exception escapes, exactly like conn.transaction(). If you see session.commit() and session.rollback() calls in a customer's code, that is the same BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK underneath.
replace_subtopics.example: A pharmacy system moves 20 units of a drug from Warehouse A to Store 14. It subtracts 20 from A and adds 20 to Store 14. If the second update fails because Store 14's row is missing, the rollback puts the 20 units back at A, and the stock total stays correct. Later the pharmacy imports a stock file of 3 rows, one with a negative quantity. With a savepoint per row, the bad row is skipped and reported, and the 2 good rows are committed.

import psycopg   # psycopg 3

def transfer_stock(conn, sku, from_loc, to_loc, qty):
    # The 'with conn.transaction()' block commits on success, rolls back on error
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute(
            "UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - %s WHERE sku = %s AND location = %s",
            (qty, sku, from_loc))
        cur = conn.execute(
            "UPDATE stock SET qty = qty + %s WHERE sku = %s AND location = %s",
            (qty, sku, to_loc))
        if cur.rowcount != 1:                  # destination row missing
            raise ValueError("unknown destination")   # triggers ROLLBACK

with psycopg.connect("postgresql://app@localhost/pharmacy") as conn:
    transfer_stock(conn, "AMOX-500", "WH-A", "STORE-14", 20)


# --- Savepoints: skip one bad row, keep the rest ---
from psycopg import errors

# Savepoints: a nested conn.transaction() creates one. A failure inside
# rolls back only to the savepoint; the outer transaction carries on.
def import_rows(conn, rows):
    skipped = []
    with conn.transaction():                    # BEGIN
        for sku, loc, qty in rows:
            try:
                with conn.transaction():        # SAVEPOINT
                    conn.execute("INSERT INTO stock_import VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
                                 (sku, loc, qty))
            except errors.CheckViolation:       # ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT
                skipped.append(sku)
    return skipped                              # COMMIT happened on exit

with psycopg.connect("postgresql://app@localhost/pharmacy", autocommit=True) as conn:
    conn.execute("CREATE TEMP TABLE stock_import (sku text, location text, qty int CHECK (qty >= 0))")
    print(import_rows(conn, [("AMOX-500", "WH-A", 80),
                             ("IBU-200", "WH-A", -5),     # bad row
                             ("PARA-500", "WH-A", 120)]))
    # ['IBU-200']
    print(conn.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM stock_import").fetchone())   # (2,)

from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://app@localhost/pharmacy")

replace_subtopics.title: Isolation levels and anomalies
replace_subtopics.body:
Isolation controls what a transaction can see of other concurrent transactions. Stronger isolation prevents more problems but can cause more waiting or retries.

In PostgreSQL, READ COMMITTED is the default: each statement sees data committed before that statement began. REPEATABLE READ gives the whole transaction one consistent snapshot. SERIALIZABLE makes the result equivalent to running transactions one after another, and aborts some transactions with a serialization error that you must retry.

The problems you are guarding against are called anomalies. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice and getting different values. A phantom is a repeated query returning new rows. A lost update is two writers overwriting each other. Write skew is two transactions each reading a condition, then writing in a way that together breaks it.

The mildest anomaly is the dirty read: seeing another transaction's changes before it commits, which might then be rolled back. The SQL standard allows dirty reads at READ UNCOMMITTED, but PostgreSQL never allows them. If you ask for READ UNCOMMITTED you silently get READ COMMITTED. Other databases, such as SQL Server with NOLOCK hints, do allow them, so ask when a customer's reports show numbers that 'never existed'.

In psycopg 3, set the level on the connection with conn.isolation_level = IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE. Writing SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL inside the block is fragile: it must be the very first statement of a transaction, and if one is already open, conn.transaction() becomes a savepoint and PostgreSQL rejects the SET.

Web apps often use optimistic concurrency instead of locks. Each row has a version number. The app reads the row and its version, the user edits for a minute with no lock held, and the save runs UPDATE ... WHERE id = %s AND version = %s, which also adds one to the version. If someone saved in between, zero rows change, and the app reloads and shows the newer data. ORMs support this directly (SQLAlchemy's version_id_col).
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital rule says at least one doctor must be on call per ward. Two doctors on the same ward each check 'is someone else on call?' at the same time, both see yes, and both go off call. That is write skew. Under SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL detects the conflict and aborts one of the two transactions. In the claims app, two agents open claim 88123 at version 1. The first saves 'call back Monday' and the version becomes 2. The second saves 'approved' against version 1, zero rows change, and the app shows the first agent's note instead of silently overwriting it.
replace_subtopics.code:
import psycopg
from psycopg import errors, IsolationLevel

def go_off_call(conn, doctor_id, ward, attempts=3):
    # Set the level on the connection. A "SET TRANSACTION" inside
    # conn.transaction() fails if a transaction is already open, because
    # the block then becomes a savepoint.
    conn.isolation_level = IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE
    for _ in range(attempts):
        try:
            with conn.transaction():
                (on_call,) = conn.execute(
                    "SELECT count(*) FROM shifts WHERE ward=%s AND on_call",
                    (ward,)).fetchone()
                if on_call < 2:
                    raise ValueError("last doctor on call")
                conn.execute("UPDATE shifts SET on_call=false WHERE doctor_id=%s",
                             (doctor_id,))
            return True
        except errors.SerializationFailure:
            continue                    # conflict detected: retry the whole transaction
    return False



# --- Optimistic concurrency with a version column ---
def save_claim_note(conn, claim_id, note, version_seen):
    # Optimistic concurrency: no lock while the user edits.
    # The write succeeds only if nobody changed the row since we read it.
    with conn.transaction():
        cur = conn.execute("""
            UPDATE claims
               SET note = %s, version = version + 1
             WHERE claim_id = %s AND version = %s
        """, (note, claim_id, version_seen))
        return cur.rowcount == 1        # False: reload and show the newer note

with psycopg.connect("postgresql://app@localhost/sandbox") as conn:
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS claims")
    conn.execute("""CREATE TABLE claims (claim_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
                    note text, version int NOT NULL DEFAULT 1)""")
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO claims (claim_id, note) VALUES (88123, 'new')")
    conn.commit()
    # Two agents both loaded version 1
    print(save_claim_note(conn, 88123, "call back Monday", 1))   # True
    print(save_claim_note(conn, 88123, "approved", 1))           # False
    print(conn.execute("SELECT note, version FROM claims").fetchone())
    # ('call back Monday', 2)

replace_subtopics.title: Normalization for transactional data
replace_subtopics.body:
Normalization, designing tables so each fact is stored once, has its own topic: see normalize (Schema design) for keys, 1NF to 3NF, junction tables and migrations.

The link to ACID is simple. A transaction guarantees that one unit of work is all or nothing, but it cannot protect a fact that is stored in many places. If a customer's address is copied onto 3,400 rows, a correct transaction can still update 3,188 of them if the code only knows about some. When each fact lives in one row, a single short transaction changes it everywhere at once, and constraints (foreign keys, UNIQUE) can check it.

So the usual design is normalized tables for the application that writes, and denormalized copies (views, materialized views or warehouse tables) for reporting and AI retrieval that mostly read.
replace_subtopics.example: A clinic stored the doctor's name and phone on every appointment row. When Dr. Rivera changed phone numbers, 3,400 rows needed updating, and 212 were missed. Moving doctor details into a doctors table referenced by doctor_id makes the change one row in one transaction.

add_glossary: Deadlock
Two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds; PostgreSQL aborts one with error 40P01.
lock_timeout
A setting that makes a statement give up if it cannot get a lock within the given time.
Savepoint
A marker inside a transaction that you can roll back to without undoing the whole transaction.
Optimistic concurrency
Saving only if a row's version number is unchanged since you read it, instead of holding a lock.
Dirty read
Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes; PostgreSQL never allows it.
Transactional outbox
Recording an external action in a table in the same transaction as the business change, for a worker to send later.
SKIP LOCKED
A FOR UPDATE option that skips rows other transactions have locked, used to build job queues in Postgres.
Saga
A multi-step business process where each step has a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails.

add_subtopics.title: When not to use Spark
add_subtopics.body:
Spark is built for data that does not fit on one machine. It pays for that with overhead: a driver, executors, shuffles over the network, cluster start-up time and a harder debugging story. Customers often ask for 'a Spark pipeline' because it sounds enterprise-grade, when their data is 2 GB. A modern laptop has 16 to 64 GB of RAM and 8 or more cores, and one cloud VM can have hundreds of GB.

A practical rule: if the data you actually process in one run (after filtering and selecting columns) is under a few tens of GB, a single-machine tool is usually faster to build, faster to run and cheaper. The main options are pandas (familiar, but single-threaded and memory-hungry), Polars (a fast DataFrame library that uses all cores) and DuckDB (an in-process SQL engine that queries Parquet and CSV files directly, even on S3, and can spill to disk when data is bigger than memory).

Choose Spark when the input is hundreds of GB or more, when it will grow there soon, when the customer already runs Databricks or EMR and wants one platform, or when you need its streaming and lakehouse features. Otherwise, start small. A DuckDB job can move to Spark later with little change, because both speak SQL.
add_subtopics.example: A logistics customer asks for Spark to build a daily revenue report. The data is 18 months of shipments, 2.3 GB of Parquet. The FDE writes the report in DuckDB: it runs in 6 seconds on a small VM, needs no cluster and costs almost nothing. A Databricks job cluster would take about 5 minutes just to start. The FDE writes the decision and the threshold in the design doc: move to Spark if a single run passes about 50 GB.

add_subtopics.title: Spark SQL, the Spark UI and Databricks basics
add_subtopics.body:
Everything you can do with the DataFrame API you can also write as SQL. Register a DataFrame as a temporary view with createOrReplaceTempView("lines"), then run spark.sql("SELECT ...") and get a DataFrame back. Both go through the same Catalyst optimizer, so there is no speed difference. Many customer analysts know SQL but not Python, so SQL is often easier to hand over.

The Spark UI is how you see what a job really did. Locally it is at localhost:4040 while the application runs; on Databricks it is behind the cluster's Spark UI link. The Jobs tab lists each action. A job is split into stages at each shuffle. The Stages tab shows every stage's tasks with duration, input size, shuffle read and write, and spill (memory and disk). The SQL / DataFrame tab draws the physical plan so you can check for a BroadcastHashJoin or confirm partition filters. Two things to look for first: spill, which means partitions are too big for memory, and skew, where the max task time is far above the median.

Databricks wraps Spark in a managed platform. Notebooks mix Python, SQL and Markdown cells. A cluster (or serverless compute) runs the code: all-purpose clusters for interactive work, job clusters that start and stop for each scheduled run and cost less. Jobs (Workflows) schedule notebooks or scripts with retries and alerts. Unity Catalog governs tables and permissions. Read-only access to the customer's workspace plus the Spark UI answers most 'why is it slow' questions.
add_subtopics.example: A retailer's nightly job on Databricks has grown from 20 to 95 minutes. The FDE opens the Spark UI for last night's run. In the Stages tab, one stage shows 199 tasks finishing in about 40 seconds and one task taking 58 minutes with 30 GB of spill: classic skew. The SQL tab shows the join as a SortMergeJoin on store_id, and store 0 turns out to be a placeholder for 'online'. Enabling AQE skew handling and filtering store 0 into its own path brings the job back to 24 minutes.

replace_subtopics.title: Driver, executors and partitions
replace_subtopics.body:
A Spark application has one driver and many executors. The driver runs your program, builds the plan and schedules work. Executors run on worker nodes, each with some CPU cores and memory, and process data.

Data is divided into partitions. Each partition is processed by one task, and one task runs on one executor core at a time. If you have 200 partitions and 50 cores, Spark runs 50 tasks, then the next 50, and so on.

Partition size matters. Aim for partitions roughly in the 100 to 200 MB range. Tiny partitions waste time on scheduling overhead. Huge ones leave cores idle and may not fit in memory.

You change the partition count with two different tools. repartition(n) does a full shuffle: every row can move, and you get n partitions of roughly equal size. It can raise or lower the count, and repartition("col") also groups rows by a column. coalesce(n) only merges existing partitions on the same executors without a shuffle, so it is cheap, but it can only reduce the count and the result may be uneven. Asking coalesce(50) on 8 partitions leaves 8. Use coalesce to cut the number of output files at the end of a job, and repartition when data is badly balanced or you need more parallelism.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer's clickstream is 400 GB of Parquet in 50,000 small files of about 8 MB each. Reading it creates tens of thousands of tiny tasks, and the job spends much of its time on scheduling. Compacting the data into about 2,500 files of 160 MB each cuts the read stage from 40 minutes to 9. At the end of a small daily job that produces 200 tiny shuffle partitions, coalesce(4) writes 4 files without another shuffle. For the 400 GB compaction above, repartition(2500) is the right tool, because the input files are uneven and a full shuffle evens them out.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .appName("clickstream-daily")
         .getOrCreate())

df = spark.read.parquet("s3://retail-lake/clickstream/2026/09/")
print("partitions:", df.rdd.getNumPartitions())   # how many tasks the read creates

# Compact many small files into fewer, larger ones (about 160 MB each)
(df.repartition(2500)
   .write.mode("overwrite")
   .parquet("s3://retail-lake/clickstream_compact/2026/09/"))

# repartition versus coalesce (checked on a local session)
df = spark.range(1_000_000)
print(df.rdd.getNumPartitions())                           # depends on cores, e.g. 2
print(df.repartition(8).rdd.getNumPartitions())            # 8: full shuffle
print(df.coalesce(1).rdd.getNumPartitions())               # 1: merge, no shuffle
print(df.repartition(8).coalesce(50).rdd.getNumPartitions())  # 8: coalesce cannot grow

replace_subtopics.title: Lazy evaluation and actions
replace_subtopics.body:
Spark operations come in two kinds. Transformations, such as filter, select, withColumn, groupBy and join, describe a new DataFrame. Actions, such as count, show, collect and write, ask for a result.

Transformations are lazy: they only add steps to a plan. Nothing runs until an action is called. This lets Spark's optimizer, called Catalyst, see the whole pipeline and improve it, for example by pushing a date filter down into the file read so fewer files are opened.

You can inspect the plan with explain(). Be careful with collect(), which brings the entire result into the driver's memory and can crash it on large data.

Reading is where many jobs go wrong before any transformation runs. With CSV, option("inferSchema", True) makes Spark read the data an extra time to guess types, which is slow on big files, and the guesses can be wrong: an id like 00042 becomes the integer 42 and loses its leading zeros, and money becomes a double. In production, pass an explicit schema built with StructType and StructField, and consider mode FAILFAST so a malformed row stops the job instead of silently turning into nulls.

JSON often arrives nested. Spark reads objects as struct columns and lists as array columns. Reach inside a struct with a dotted name such as customer.address.city, and turn each array element into its own row with F.explode. printSchema() shows the tree so you know the paths.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer filters 5 years of claims to September 2026 and selects 4 of 60 columns. Because Parquet stores columns separately and the data is partitioned by month, Catalyst reads only September's folder and only 4 columns. The job reads about 3 GB instead of 1.2 TB. The same insurer receives a CSV where claim ids have leading zeros. With inferSchema, 00042 became 42 and failed to match the policy system. An explicit schema keeps claim_id as a string and amount as DECIMAL(12,2).

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

claims = spark.read.parquet("s3://ins-lake/claims/")     # nothing read yet

sept = (claims
        .filter(F.col("claim_month") == "2026-09")     # transformation (lazy)
        .select("claim_id", "policy_id", "amount", "status"))

sept.explain()          # shows PartitionFilters and pruned columns in the plan

print(sept.count())     # action: now Spark actually runs the job

# Avoid on big data: pulls every row into the driver
# rows = sept.collect()
sample = sept.limit(20).toPandas()   # safe: small, bounded result

# Explicit schema instead of inferSchema (CSV)

                               DecimalType, DateType)
schema = StructType([
    StructField("claim_id",   StringType(),       False),  # keeps "00042"
    StructField("policy_id",  StringType(),       True),
    StructField("amount",     DecimalType(12, 2), True),   # money, not double
    StructField("claim_date", DateType(),         True),
    StructField("status",     StringType(),       True),
])
claims_csv = (spark.read.option("header", True)
              .option("mode", "FAILFAST")        # stop on malformed rows
              .schema(schema)
              .csv("s3://ins-lake/landing/claims_2026-09.csv"))

events.printSchema()

         .select("id", F.col("customer.address.city").alias("city"),
                 F.explode("items").alias("item"))
         .select("id", "city", "item.sku", "item.qty"))

replace_subtopics.title: Joins: broadcast and skew
replace_subtopics.body:
Joining two large tables requires shuffling both by the join key. If one side is small, Spark can instead copy it to every executor. This is a broadcast join, and the large side never moves. Spark does this automatically below a size threshold, and you can force it with F.broadcast().

Skew means a few keys have far more rows than the rest. After a shuffle, the task holding a hot key does most of the work while other tasks finish and wait. In the Spark UI, you see most tasks take seconds and one take an hour.

Fixes include AQE's skew join handling, which splits oversized partitions, and salting: adding a random number to the hot key so its rows spread across several partitions, then combining the results.

Salting a join takes one more step than salting an aggregation. On the big, skewed side, add a random salt from 0 to N-1 to each row. On the small side, make N copies of every row, one for each salt value, with crossJoin against a range of N. Then join on both the key and the salt. Every big-side row still finds exactly one matching copy, but the hot key's rows now go to N different tasks. The cost is that the small side grows N times, so keep N modest (8 to 32).
replace_subtopics.example: A food delivery platform joins 3 billion order events to a 40 MB restaurants table. Broadcasting the restaurants table removes a shuffle of the big table. Separately, a join on city is skewed because one metro area has 35 percent of orders. Salting city into 16 buckets spreads that load across 16 tasks. For the skewed join on city, the city lookup table (a few hundred rows) is copied 16 times, and orders get a salt from 0 to 15. The metro area's rows now spread over 16 tasks. A local test with 1,000 orders confirms the salted join still returns 1,000 rows.
replace_subtopics.code:
orders = spark.read.parquet("s3://food-lake/orders/")          # about 3 billion rows
restaurants = spark.read.parquet("s3://food-lake/restaurants/") # about 40 MB

# Broadcast join: copy the small side to every executor, no big shuffle
enriched = orders.join(F.broadcast(restaurants), "restaurant_id")

# Let AQE split skewed partitions automatically
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")

# Manual salting for a skewed aggregation on city
N = 16
salted = orders.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))
partial = salted.groupBy("city", "salt").agg(F.sum("total").alias("part"))
by_city = partial.groupBy("city").agg(F.sum("part").alias("gmv"))   # combine salts

# Manual salting for a skewed JOIN on city: explode the small side
cities = spark.read.parquet("s3://food-lake/cities/")     # small: city -> country
orders_s = orders.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))   # 0..N-1
cities_s = cities.crossJoin(                               # N copies per city
    spark.range(N).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt"))
joined = orders_s.join(cities_s, ["city", "salt"]).drop("salt")
# Same row count as an unsalted join; the hot city now spans N tasks

replace_subtopics.title: Writing output for fast reads
replace_subtopics.body:
How you write data decides how fast the next job can read it. Parquet is a columnar file format, which stores each column separately and compresses well, so readers can skip columns they do not need.

partitionBy on write creates one folder per value, such as region=EU. Readers that filter on region then skip whole folders. Choose a partition column with a modest number of values that queries filter on often. Partitioning by a high-cardinality column like user_id creates millions of tiny files.

Spark writes at least one file per task per output partition. Control file counts with repartition or coalesce before writing.

For comparison, Hadoop MapReduce, Spark's predecessor, wrote intermediate results to disk between every step. Spark keeps intermediate data in memory where it can, which is a main reason it is faster for multi-step jobs.

A classic data-loss trap: mode("overwrite") together with partitionBy replaces the whole output folder by default. Rerunning one day, for example to fix 2026-09-26, deletes every other date. Set spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode to dynamic, so an overwrite replaces only the partitions present in the new data. Test it on a copy first.

Plain Parquet folders have other limits: no safe updates of single rows, and readers can see half-written files. Most new lakehouses therefore write to a table format, Delta Lake (Databricks) or Apache Iceberg (Snowflake, AWS, others), which adds a transaction log on top of Parquet. You get MERGE INTO for upserts, OPTIMIZE to compact small files (plus Z-ORDER or clustering on Delta), and time travel to query or restore an earlier version. See warehouse for the lakehouse overview.
replace_subtopics.example: A marketing analytics customer writes daily spend per campaign partitioned by date and region, with 6 regions. A dashboard query for 'EU, last 7 days' reads 7 folders out of thousands. Before, the table was partitioned by campaign_id with 90,000 values and produced over a million small files. On the Spark 4 test run, rewriting only 2026-09-26 with the default static mode left a single folder, event_date=2026-09-26, and the 25th was gone. With dynamic mode both dates remained and only the 26th changed. The customer later moved the table to Delta and replaced the daily rewrite with a MERGE on (event_date, region, campaign_id).

daily = (spark.read.parquet("s3://mkt-lake/ad_events/")
         .groupBy("event_date", "region", "campaign_id")
         .agg(F.sum("cost").alias("spend"), F.sum("clicks").alias("clicks")))

(daily
   .repartition("event_date", "region")     # one task per folder: fewer, larger files
   .write
   .mode("overwrite")
   .partitionBy("event_date", "region")     # folders like event_date=2026-09-26/region=EU/
   .parquet("s3://mkt-lake/marts/daily_spend/"))

# Reader: only matching folders are scanned
eu_week = (spark.read.parquet("s3://mkt-lake/marts/daily_spend/")
           .filter((F.col("region") == "EU") & (F.col("event_date") >= "2026-09-20")))

# Data-loss trap: without this, overwrite + partitionBy deletes ALL dates
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
fix_26th = daily.filter(F.col("event_date") == "2026-09-26")
(fix_26th.write.mode("overwrite")
    .partitionBy("event_date", "region")
    .parquet("s3://mkt-lake/marts/daily_spend/"))   # only 2026-09-26 replaced

spark.sql("""
  MERGE INTO marts.daily_spend t
  USING updates u
    ON t.event_date = u.event_date AND t.region = u.region
   AND t.campaign_id = u.campaign_id
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
""")
spark.sql("OPTIMIZE marts.daily_spend ZORDER BY (campaign_id)")   # compaction
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM marts.daily_spend VERSION AS OF 12")    # time travel

add_subtopics.title: Buy before you build: managed connectors
add_subtopics.body:
Before writing an extractor, check whether someone has already built and maintains it. Managed connector tools copy data from common sources into a warehouse for you. Fivetran is the best-known paid service with hundreds of ready connectors. Airbyte is open source with a hosted option. dlt (data load tool) is an open-source Python library: you write a small generator and it handles schema inference, incremental cursors and loading. The clouds have their own: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) replicates databases, including CDC, and Azure Data Factory and Google Cloud's Datastream do similar jobs.

A managed connector usually wins for standard SaaS sources such as Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, Stripe or NetSuite. Their APIs change, paginate strangely and rate-limit, and a vendor with thousands of customers fixes those problems before you notice them. You also get schema drift handling, retries and monitoring for free.

Custom code wins in other cases. On-premises legacy systems (an AS/400, an old Oracle behind a firewall) often have no connector or need network access a SaaS tool cannot get. Custom internal APIs have no connector at all. Some customers forbid data passing through a third-party service, and per-row pricing can become expensive at very high volumes.

A useful habit: list every source in the first week, mark each as connector available or custom, and estimate the monthly cost of the connector against the days of engineering it replaces. dlt is a good middle path when you need code but want the boring parts done for you.
add_subtopics.example: A software company, Brightline Analytics, needs Zendesk tickets, Salesforce opportunities and an in-house licensing database in Snowflake for a churn assistant. Fivetran connectors for Zendesk and Salesforce are running in one afternoon. The licensing database sits behind the company VPN with no connector, so the FDE writes a 60-line dlt pipeline that runs inside their network, with a merge on the primary key and an incremental cursor on updated_at.

# A resource is any Python generator. dlt infers the schema, creates tables,
# and remembers the incremental cursor between runs for you.

def tickets(updated_at=dlt.sources.incremental("updated_at", initial_value="2026-01-01")):
    # In real life: page through the helpdesk API here with requests
    page = [
        {"ticket_id": 1, "status": "open",   "updated_at": "2026-03-01"},
        {"ticket_id": 2, "status": "closed", "updated_at": "2026-03-02"},
    ]
    yield page

pipeline = dlt.pipeline(pipeline_name="helpdesk", destination="duckdb",
                        dataset_name="bronze")
print(pipeline.run(tickets()))     # load summary: packages, tables, rows
with pipeline.sql_client() as c:
    print(c.execute_sql("SELECT ticket_id, status FROM tickets ORDER BY 1"))

replace_subtopics.title: Extracting: full loads and watermarks
replace_subtopics.body:
Extraction means reading data out of a source system. The first time, you usually do a full load: copy every row. That is fine once, but copying a 200 million row table every night is slow and puts load on the customer's production database.

After the first load you switch to incremental extraction. The most common method is a watermark: a column such as updated_at that tells you when each row last changed. You remember the highest value you have already copied, and next time you only ask for rows changed since then.

A strict updated_at > watermark filter has two holes. First, ties: two rows can share the same timestamp, and if only one was committed when you last read, the other is skipped forever. Second, late commits: a long transaction can commit a row whose updated_at is a few minutes older than your watermark. The safe pattern is to read with >= and a small look-back overlap (for example 10 minutes before the watermark), then remove the repeated rows with a dedupe step or a MERGE on the key. Re-reading a few rows is cheap; losing one is not. Store and compare timestamps in UTC so a daylight-saving change cannot shift your window by an hour.

Set the new watermark to the largest updated_at you actually received, not to the clock time, and save it only after the load succeeds.

A watermark query cannot see deletes, because a deleted row is simply gone. Without CDC you have two options. Ask whether the source uses a soft-delete flag (is_deleted or deleted_at), which is just another update the watermark catches. Otherwise, run a periodic full key comparison: pull only the primary keys from the source, compare them with your keys, and mark the missing ones as deleted.

A stronger option is change data capture (CDC). CDC reads the database's own transaction log, so it also sees deletes. Tools such as Debezium or a cloud provider's replication service do this for you.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer, Larkfield Stores, keeps orders in PostgreSQL. On day one you copy all 12 million orders. You store the watermark 2026-03-01 23:59:58 UTC. The next night you ask for orders with updated_at at or after 23:49:58 (the 10 minute overlap) and receive 41,300 rows in a few seconds, including order 3 which shares the exact 23:59:58 timestamp and would have been skipped by a strict greater-than filter. The MERGE into silver removes the few rows you had already seen. You save the new watermark only after the load succeeds, so a failed run simply retries the same window. Every Sunday a key comparison finds 212 order ids that no longer exist in the source and marks them deleted.

import json, pathlib
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import psycopg                      # psycopg 3
from psycopg.rows import dict_row   # rows come back as dicts, with column names

STATE = pathlib.Path("state/orders_watermark.json")
OVERLAP = timedelta(minutes=10)     # re-read the last 10 minutes every run

def read_watermark() -> datetime:
    # Default to the start of time on the very first (full) load
    if STATE.exists():
        return datetime.fromisoformat(json.loads(STATE.read_text())["updated_at"])
    return datetime(1970, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)

def extract_orders(conn_str: str):
    wm = read_watermark()
    since = wm - OVERLAP            # look back a little to catch late commits
    with psycopg.connect(conn_str, row_factory=dict_row) as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE updated_at >= %s ORDER BY updated_at",
            (since,),               # parameterized, never string-formatted
        ).fetchall()
    # New watermark = newest change we actually saw (or the old one if none)
    new_wm = max((r["updated_at"] for r in rows), default=wm)
    return rows, new_wm

def save_watermark(new_wm: datetime) -> None:
    # Call this only AFTER the load step succeeded
    STATE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    STATE.write_text(json.dumps({"updated_at": new_wm.isoformat()}))

replace_subtopics.title: Landing raw data in layers
replace_subtopics.body:
In ELT you save exactly what you extracted, unchanged, before doing anything else. This raw copy is your safety net. If a transformation has a bug, you fix the code and rerun it over the raw data instead of asking the customer for another export.

Many teams name their layers with the medallion pattern. Bronze holds raw data as it landed. Silver holds cleaned data with correct types and no duplicates. Gold holds business-ready tables, often called marts, organized around topics such as orders or claims.

Raw data is commonly stored as Parquet files, a compressed column-based file format, split into folders by date. Splitting data into folders like this is called partitioning, and it lets later jobs read only the days they need.

Two details trip people up in the landing code. pandas does not create missing folders, so writing to a new load_date= folder fails with FileNotFoundError unless you create the folder first with pathlib. And record the load time in UTC with pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC"); the older pd.Timestamp.utcnow() is deprecated in recent pandas versions. Pass the load date in from the scheduler rather than reading today's date, so a rerun for last Tuesday writes into last Tuesday's folder.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer, Harbor Mutual, sends a nightly claims extract. You write it to bronze/claims/load_date=2026-03-02/part-0.parquet. Two weeks later you discover the claim_amount column was parsed as text. You fix the silver transformation and rebuild 14 days of silver data from bronze in minutes, without touching the insurer's systems.

import pathlib
import pandas as pd
from datetime import date

def land_raw(rows: list[dict], table: str, lake_root: str = "lake",
             load_date: str | None = None) -> str:
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)                        # dict rows keep column names
    df["_loaded_at"] = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")  # audit column, always UTC
    load_date = load_date or date.today().isoformat()
    path = f"{lake_root}/bronze/{table}/load_date={load_date}"
    pathlib.Path(path).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # pandas will not create it
    # One folder per day = one partition. Rerunning overwrites that day only.
    df.to_parquet(f"{path}/part-0.parquet", index=False)   # needs pyarrow
    return path

p = land_raw([{"claim_id": "C-1", "amount": "120.50"}], "claims", load_date="2026-03-02")
print(p)                                           # lake/bronze/claims/load_date=2026-03-02
print(pd.read_parquet(p).columns.tolist())         # ['claim_id', 'amount', '_loaded_at']

replace_subtopics.title: Data quality tests and freshness
replace_subtopics.body:
Data quality tests are small checks that run after each transformation. They catch problems before a business user or an AI agent sees them.

Start with four kinds. Not-null checks that required columns are filled. Uniqueness checks that keys appear once. Referential integrity checks that every foreign key points to a real row, for example every order's customer_id exists in customers. Freshness checks that the newest row is recent enough, so a stalled pipeline raises an alert instead of silently serving old data.

In dbt you declare these tests in a YAML file next to your models. A failing test stops downstream models from building, which is exactly what you want. dbt 1.10 and later expect test settings such as to and field under an arguments: key; older projects put them directly under relationships:. Both forms still work, and you will see both in customer repositories.

Two more checks compare the pipeline with the outside world. Row-count reconciliation asks the source how many rows changed in the window (SELECT COUNT(*) with the same filter) and compares that with the number you loaded. A mismatch means rows were lost or duplicated on the way. A volume anomaly check compares today's count with the average of the last 7 days: an orders feed that usually brings about 41,000 rows and today brings 3,000 is probably broken, even though every row in it passes not-null and unique. Alert when the count falls outside a band, such as 50 percent either side of the average.

For profiling a new source, amount and total reconciliation, expectation suites and matching records across systems, see the Data quality topic (dataquality), which goes deeper than this pipeline view.
replace_subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual's claims assistant answers 'What is the status of claim C-55120?'. One Monday the extract job silently stopped, and the assistant kept answering from Friday's data. A freshness rule that warns after 12 hours and errors after 24 hours would have paged the on-call engineer on Saturday morning. A month later a source-side filter change made the nightly extract return 3,150 claims instead of the usual 41,000. Every test passed because the rows themselves were fine, but the volume check raised an alert before the morning claims meeting.

# models/schema.yml (dbt). Recent dbt versions call the key data_tests;
# older versions use tests. dbt 1.10+ puts test settings under arguments:
version: 2
sources:
  - name: bronze
    tables:
      - name: claims
        loaded_at_field: _loaded_at
        freshness:
          warn_after:  {count: 12, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
models:
  - name: claims
    columns:
      - name: claim_id
        data_tests: [not_null, unique]
      - name: policy_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:          # every claim points at a real policy
              arguments:            # older dbt: put to and field directly here
                to: ref('policies')
                field: policy_id

# ---- Python: reconciliation and volume checks after the load ----
def check_row_counts(source_count: int, loaded_count: int) -> None:
    # Reconciliation: every row the source says changed must have landed
    if source_count != loaded_count:
        raise ValueError(f"row count mismatch: source {source_count}, loaded {loaded_count}")

def check_volume(today: int, last_7_days: list[int], tolerance: float = 0.5) -> str:
    # Volume anomaly: compare today's count with the 7-day average
    avg = sum(last_7_days) / len(last_7_days)
    low, high = avg * (1 - tolerance), avg * (1 + tolerance)
    if not low <= today <= high:
        return f"ALERT: {today} rows, expected {low:.0f} to {high:.0f}"
    return f"ok: {today} rows (7-day average {avg:.0f})"

check_row_counts(41_300, 41_300)                  # passes silently
history = [40_100, 41_900, 39_800, 42_300, 40_700, 41_200, 40_600]
print(check_volume(41_300, history))   # ok: 41300 rows (7-day average 40943)
print(check_volume(3_150, history))    # ALERT: 3150 rows, expected 20471 to 61414

replace_subtopics.title: Orchestrating the whole pipeline
replace_subtopics.body:
An orchestrator is a scheduler that runs the steps of a pipeline in order, retries failures and shows you what happened. Apache Airflow is the most common one. Dagster and Prefect are popular alternatives, and cloud warehouses have their own simpler schedulers.

In Airflow a pipeline is a DAG, short for directed acyclic graph: a set of tasks with arrows showing which must finish before which, and no loops. You write it in Python. Each task should be small and idempotent so a retry is safe. Airflow 3, released in 2025, moved the TaskFlow imports to from airflow.sdk import dag, task. Airflow 2 projects use from airflow.decorators import dag, task. Check which version the customer runs before copying examples.

Every scheduled run covers a time window, the data interval, and Airflow tells each task where its window starts and ends (the logical date is its start). Use those values instead of the current date, so each run processes its own window. Catchup decides what happens when a DAG is switched on with a start_date in the past: with catchup=True Airflow creates a run for every missed interval, and with catchup=False it runs only the latest. A backfill is a deliberate re-run of a date range, for example after fixing a bug: airflow backfill create --dag-id larkfield_orders --from-date 2026-03-01 --to-date 2026-03-07 on Airflow 3, or airflow dags backfill -s 2026-03-01 -e 2026-03-07 larkfield_orders on Airflow 2. Backfills are only safe when loads are idempotent.

When choosing ETL versus ELT, ask where sensitive data may land. If regulations say patient names must be masked before they leave the hospital's network, you transform first (ETL). That transform usually means replacing identifiers with tokens from a keyed hash, so the same patient still joins across tables, coarsening dates of birth to a year, and dropping free-text fields, which often hide names and diagnoses. Keep the hashing key in the customer's secret store. Otherwise ELT is usually simpler and keeps a replayable raw copy.
replace_subtopics.example: For Larkfield the daily DAG runs at 02:00: extract orders, mask PII, land them in bronze for the run's own date, run dbt to build silver and gold with tests, and only then save the new watermark. If extract fails, Airflow retries it three times, five minutes apart, and the downstream tasks wait; the watermark is untouched, so the next attempt reads the same window. After a bug fix in the silver model, the team backfills 1 to 7 March and each run writes into its own load_date folder. At Riverside Health the mask step turns NHS numbers into 16-character tokens before anything leaves the hospital network.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from airflow.sdk import dag, task            # Airflow 3 (released 2025)
# Airflow 2.x used: from airflow.decorators import dag, task

@dag(schedule="0 2 * * *", start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
     catchup=False,                          # do not auto-run every missed day
     default_args={"retries": 3, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)})
def larkfield_orders():

    @task
    def extract(data_interval_end=None) -> dict:
        # Airflow passes the run's own window end: use it, not "today",
        # so a backfill of 3 March writes into the 3 March partition.
        rows, new_wm = extract_orders(CONN)            # dict rows, UTC watermark
        rows = mask_pii(rows)                          # the T before the L (ETL)
        path = land_raw(rows, "orders", load_date=data_interval_end.date().isoformat())
        return {"path": path, "new_wm": new_wm.isoformat(), "count": len(rows)}

    @task
    def transform(info: dict) -> dict:
        import subprocess
        # dbt build = run models + run tests, stops on failure
        subprocess.run(["dbt", "build", "--select", "orders+"], check=True)
        return info

    @task
    def commit_watermark(info: dict) -> None:
        # Runs only if everything above succeeded, so a failed run
        # simply re-reads the same window next time.
        save_watermark(datetime.fromisoformat(info["new_wm"]))

    commit_watermark(transform(extract()))   # extract -> transform -> commit

larkfield_orders()

# ---- mask_pii: the T of ETL, run before data leaves the network ----
import hashlib, hmac, os
import pandas as pd

# The secret lives in the customer's vault, never in code or in the lake.
KEY = os.environ.get("PII_HASH_KEY", "dev-only-key").encode()

def tokenize(value: str) -> str:
    # Keyed hash (HMAC): the same patient always gets the same token, so joins
    # still work, but nobody without the key can reverse or rebuild it.
    return hmac.new(KEY, value.strip().lower().encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:16]

def mask_patients(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    out = df.copy()
    out["patient_token"] = out["nhs_number"].map(tokenize)   # identifier -> token
    out["birth_year"] = pd.to_datetime(out["date_of_birth"]).dt.year  # coarsen
    # Drop direct identifiers and free text, which can hide names and diagnoses
    return out.drop(columns=["nhs_number", "patient_name", "date_of_birth", "notes"])

raw = pd.DataFrame({
    "nhs_number": ["943 476 5919", "943 476 5919"],
    "patient_name": ["Ana Silva", "Ana Silva"],
    "date_of_birth": ["1984-05-02", "1984-05-02"],
    "notes": ["called about knee pain", "follow-up booked"],
    "appointment_id": [501, 502],
})
print(mask_patients(raw).columns.tolist())
# ['appointment_id', 'patient_token', 'birth_year']
print(mask_patients(raw)["patient_token"].nunique())   # 1: same patient, same token

add_glossary: Look-back overlap
Re-reading a short period before the watermark on each run so late or tied rows are not missed.
Soft delete
Marking a row as deleted with a flag or deleted_at column instead of removing it, so incremental loads can see the deletion.
Data interval
The time window a scheduled run is responsible for; Airflow passes its start and end to each task.
Backfill
Deliberately re-running a pipeline for a past date range, for example after fixing a bug.
Catchup
An Airflow setting that decides whether missed past intervals are run automatically when a DAG starts.
Row-count reconciliation
Comparing the number of rows the source reports with the number the pipeline loaded.
Volume anomaly check
Alerting when today's row count is far from its recent average.
Tokenization
Replacing an identifier with a consistent stand-in value, for example a keyed hash, so data can be joined without exposing the original.
Managed connector
A maintained service or library, such as Fivetran, Airbyte or dlt, that extracts data from a known source into a warehouse.

add_subtopics.title: dbt materializations and incremental models
add_subtopics.body:
A materialization is how dbt turns a model's SELECT into something in the warehouse. There are four main kinds.

A view stores only the query. It costs nothing to build and is always current, but every read reruns the query, so it suits light staging models. A table runs the query and stores the result, dropping and rebuilding it on every run. Reads are fast, but rebuilding a 2 billion row fact table every hour is slow and expensive. An ephemeral model is never created in the warehouse at all: dbt pastes it into the models that use it as a CTE, which keeps small helper logic out of the schema.

An incremental model is built in full the first time and afterwards only processes new or changed rows. Inside the model, is_incremental() is true on those later runs, so you add a WHERE filter such as updated_at >= the newest value already in the table, referred to as {{ this }}. You also set unique_key, and dbt uses an incremental strategy to fold the new rows in. merge updates matching keys and inserts new ones. delete+insert removes matching keys and re-inserts them. append only adds rows and suits event logs with no updates. insert_overwrite replaces whole partitions. Which strategies exist depends on the platform adapter.

Use >= rather than > in the filter for the same reason as in the etl topic: rows that share the newest timestamp are not lost, and the unique_key merge removes the repeats. When the logic changes, or a bug corrupted history, run dbt run --full-refresh --select the_model to rebuild it from scratch.
add_subtopics.example: A delivery company's fct_deliveries has 1.8 billion rows. As a table it took 55 minutes and a large warehouse to rebuild every hour. Converted to incremental with unique_key='delivery_id' and a merge strategy, each hourly run reads about 90,000 changed rows and finishes in 40 seconds. When a currency bug is fixed in March, one full refresh rebuilds history overnight.

rows: Small or medium marts read often

  -- only on later runs: rows changed since the newest row already in the table
  -- ({{ this }} is the existing fct_orders table)
  where updated_at >= (select max(updated_at) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

add_subtopics.title: Access control and cost on a warehouse
add_subtopics.body:
Two questions come up in every warehouse engagement: who may see what, and who pays for it.

Access is granted to roles, never directly to people. You create a role such as assistant_reader, grant it usage on a database and schema and SELECT on tables, then grant the role to a user or service account. Grant SELECT on future tables too, or the next new table will be invisible. An AI assistant should get its own read-only role limited to the marts it needs.

Personal data needs finer control. A column masking policy returns the real value only to approved roles and a masked value to everyone else, so an email column shows ***MASKED*** to analysts. A row access policy filters rows by the caller, so each regional manager sees only their region. Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks all offer both, with different syntax. Test them by switching to the role and running a query, not by reading the policy.

Cost follows the pricing model. Snowflake bills credits for the time a virtual warehouse runs, and doubling the size doubles the credits per hour. Start at XSMALL, set AUTO_SUSPEND to 60 seconds so an idle warehouse stops billing, and give each workload its own warehouse. BigQuery on-demand pricing charges per byte scanned, so partitioning, clustering, dry runs and a maximum_bytes_billed limit matter. Capacity pricing buys slots, units of compute, for a fixed price instead. To see which project spent what, tag queries: QUERY_TAG in Snowflake or job labels in BigQuery, then group the usage views by tag.
add_subtopics.example: At Harbor Mutual the claims assistant uses a service user with the role assistant_reader on the marts schema only. Policyholder emails are masked for every role except PII_ADMIN, and a row policy limits each broker portal to its own region. The assistant runs on its own XSMALL warehouse with 60 second auto-suspend and the query tag project:claims-assistant, so the monthly cost report shows it used 41 credits.
checklist: Each app or agent has its own role and service user
Read-only grants, including FUTURE TABLES
PII columns have masking policies
Row policies tested by switching role
Warehouse size starts small, auto-suspend 60 seconds
Query tags or labels on every workload
BigQuery: maximum_bytes_billed on ad hoc queries

replace_subtopics.title: The main platforms and the lakehouse
replace_subtopics.body:
Four names come up constantly. Snowflake is a cloud warehouse that separates storage from compute: data sits in cloud storage and you start 'virtual warehouses' of different sizes to query it. Google BigQuery is serverless: you do not size machines at all and can pay per data scanned or reserve capacity. Amazon Redshift is AWS's warehouse, available as provisioned clusters or a serverless option. Databricks started from Apache Spark and runs SQL, Python and machine learning over data in open file formats.

A data lake is cheap object storage (S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, Google Cloud Storage) full of files, often Parquet, a columnar file format. Lakes are cheap and flexible but plain files lack transactions and can become messy.

A lakehouse puts a table format such as Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg on top of the lake. The table format adds transactions, schema rules and time travel (querying a table as it was earlier), so files in object storage behave like warehouse tables. Databricks is built around this idea, and Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift can also read Iceberg tables. For an FDE, the practical lesson is to learn which platform the customer uses and work inside it.

To query a warehouse from Python, each platform has an official library. snowflake-connector-python connects to Snowflake, google-cloud-bigquery to BigQuery, and databricks-sql-connector to a Databricks SQL warehouse. All three can hand results to pandas. Two habits keep this safe. Select only the columns you need and add a WHERE filter and a LIMIT while exploring, because pulling a 2 billion row table into a laptop's memory crashes the notebook and, on per-byte pricing, costs real money. And never put passwords or tokens in code: use single sign-on for yourself, and key-pair authentication, a service account or a secret store for jobs.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer keeps clickstream events as Parquet files in S3 and sales data in Snowflake. Instead of copying billions of click rows into Snowflake, the data team registers the S3 files as an Iceberg table, and the same SQL joins clicks to sales, while their Databricks notebooks read the very same Iceberg table for model training. An FDE exploring the retailer's data first runs the query with LIMIT 10000 into pandas, checks the column types, and only then writes the full aggregation as SQL so the warehouse, not the laptop, does the heavy work.

replace_subtopics.title: dbt models, tests and lineage
replace_subtopics.body:
In dbt, each model is a .sql file containing one SELECT. dbt wraps it in the CREATE VIEW or CREATE TABLE statement for you, based on the model's materialization setting. Instead of hard-coding table names, a model refers to raw tables with source('shop', 'orders') and to other models with ref('stg_orders').

Those ref() calls are how dbt learns the dependency graph, also called lineage. dbt runs models in the right order, can run just one model and everything downstream of it, and draws the graph in its generated documentation. Projects are usually layered: staging models clean one source table each, intermediate models combine them, and marts are the final facts and dimensions people query.

Tests are declared in YAML next to the models. The four built-in generic tests are unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships (every foreign key exists in the parent table). 'dbt build' runs models and their tests together and stops downstream models when a test fails, so bad data does not reach the dashboard.

A dbt project is a folder with a few standard parts. dbt_project.yml names the project, says where models, seeds and macros live, and sets defaults such as materialized: view. profiles.yml, usually kept in ~/.dbt/ and outside git, holds the connection: warehouse type, account, database, role and which target (dev or prod) to use. The models/ folder holds the .sql files and their YAML. seeds/ holds small CSV files, such as a country code mapping, that dbt seed loads as tables. macros/ holds reusable SQL snippets written in Jinja, a templating language: {{ ... }} prints a value, such as ref('x') or a macro call, and {% if ... %} adds logic.

The everyday commands are dbt run (build models), dbt test (run tests), dbt build (seeds, models, snapshots and tests in order), dbt seed, dbt docs generate followed by dbt docs serve (the lineage site), and dbt ls to list what a selection matches. --select picks models: --select fct_orders is one model, fct_orders+ adds everything downstream, +fct_orders adds everything upstream, and tag:finance picks by tag.

Older dbt projects write test settings such as to and field directly under relationships:. dbt 1.10 and later expect them under arguments:, as shown here. Both work, and the etl topic shows the same test in the new form.
