add_subtopics.title: Settings, lifespan and app structure
add_subtopics.body:
A real service needs three things the first-endpoint example skips: configuration, shared resources and a tidy layout.

Configuration comes from the environment, never from values typed into the code. The pydantic-settings package gives you a BaseSettings class. You declare fields with types and defaults, and each field is filled from the environment variable of the same name (vendor_url reads VENDOR_URL), or from a .env file. A missing or badly typed value fails at startup with a clear message, which beats a crash at 3 a.m.

Shared resources, such as an HTTP client, a database engine or a loaded model, should be created once and closed properly. FastAPI offers a lifespan function for this. It is an async context manager: code before yield runs once at startup, code after yield runs once at shutdown. A module-level client that is never closed leaks connections. Store the shared objects on app.state and read them from request.app.state.

As the app grows, split endpoints into files and give each an APIRouter, then attach them with app.include_router. Add exception handlers with @app.exception_handler so every error leaves your API in the same JSON shape, instead of some errors being HTML and others being text.

CORS is a browser rule. If a web page served from one origin (for example https://portal.example) calls your API on another origin (https://api.example), the browser blocks the reply unless the API sends the right Access-Control headers. CORSMiddleware sends them. List the exact origins you trust; allow_origins=["*"] is only for local experiments. CORS does not protect your API from other programs. It only affects browsers, so you still need authentication.
add_subtopics.example: Crestline Freight's tracking portal runs at https://portal.crestline.example and calls the API at https://api.crestline.example. Without CORSMiddleware, the browser console shows a CORS error even though curl works fine. After adding the portal to allowed_origins, the calls succeed. When the vendor is unreachable, the handler returns a 502 with {"error": "vendor_unavailable"} instead of a raw stack trace.
add_subtopics.code:
# app.py   settings, lifespan, routers, error handler, CORS
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

import httpx
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")   # env vars win over .env
    vendor_url: str = "https://api.vendor.example"
    request_timeout: float = 10.0
    allowed_origins: list[str] = ["http://localhost:3000"]

settings = Settings()

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Runs once at startup: create shared things here
    app.state.http = httpx.AsyncClient(
        base_url=settings.vendor_url, timeout=settings.request_timeout
    )
    yield                                  # the app serves requests here
    await app.state.http.aclose()          # runs once at shutdown

class VendorDown(Exception):
    pass

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

app.add_middleware(                        # lets a browser front end on another
    CORSMiddleware,                        # origin call this API
    allow_origins=settings.allowed_origins,
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
)

@app.exception_handler(VendorDown)
async def vendor_down_handler(request: Request, exc: VendorDown):
    return JSONResponse(status_code=502,
                        content={"error": "vendor_unavailable", "detail": str(exc)})

# In a real project this router lives in routers/health.py
health = APIRouter(prefix="/health", tags=["health"])

@health.get("/vendor")
async def vendor_health(request: Request):
    try:
        r = await request.app.state.http.get("/status")
    except httpx.HTTPError as exc:
        raise VendorDown(str(exc)) from exc
    return {"vendor_status": r.status_code}

app.include_router(health)

add_subtopics.title: File uploads and long-running jobs
add_subtopics.body:
Customers often send documents: PDFs of contracts, CSV exports. FastAPI receives them with UploadFile and File(...). You need the python-multipart package installed, because uploads use the multipart/form-data format. UploadFile gives you the filename, the content_type and an async read() method.

Never trust an upload. Check the content type, and limit the size. Read at most one byte more than your limit, then reject the request with 413 if you got more. Remember that a client can lie about the content type, so real systems also check the file's first bytes. Then check the contents: a CSV with the wrong columns or empty required fields should be rejected early with a clear message (see the dataquality lesson for how to define those checks).

A slow job must not hold the HTTP request open. A proxy or load balancer will often cut a request after 30 to 60 seconds, and the user learns nothing. The standard pattern is: accept the file, create a job record, reply at once with 202 Accepted and a job id, then let the client poll GET /jobs/{id} until the status is done or failed.

For short work (a few seconds, such as sending an email), BackgroundTasks is enough. It runs after the response is sent, inside the same process. It is not durable: if the pod restarts, the work is lost, and nothing retries it. For minute-long LLM or document jobs, put a message on a queue (Celery, RQ, or a cloud queue such as SQS) and let separate workers process it. Store job status in a database or Redis, not in a Python dict like the demo below, because a dict is lost on restart and is not shared between workers.
add_subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual uploads a 40-page claim PDF. The API answers in milliseconds with 202 and {"job_id": "...", "status_url": "/jobs/..."}. The portal polls every 3 seconds and shows a progress message. A 12 MB file gets a 413, and an .exe gets a 415.

add_subtopics.title: A real database: SQLAlchemy sessions and Alembic
add_subtopics.body:
Earlier examples used a dictionary as a fake database, and the dependency example called SessionLocal without defining it. Here is the full setup with SQLAlchemy 2.0, the standard Python toolkit for talking to relational databases.

Four pieces work together. The engine holds the connection pool: a set of open connections that are reused, so each request does not pay for a fresh login. A model class (here Ticket) maps a Python class to a table. A sessionmaker creates sessions, and a session is one unit of work: you add objects, then commit to save them or roll back to undo. The get_db dependency opens one session per request and closes it afterwards, so connections always return to the pool.

Use the sync version with ordinary def endpoints. FastAPI runs those in a thread pool, so blocking database calls do not freeze the server. Use the async version (create_async_engine with a driver such as asyncpg) with async def endpoints. Never call a sync session inside async def, because it blocks the event loop. Pick one style per service and stay with it.

For responses, a Pydantic model with from_attributes=True can read fields straight from a SQLAlchemy object.

Do not call create_all in production. It only creates missing tables and never changes existing ones. Use Alembic, the migration tool for SQLAlchemy. alembic init creates a folder, alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add status column" writes a numbered script, and alembic upgrade head applies it. Always read the generated script before running it; autogenerate can miss renames and will show them as a drop plus an add, which destroys data. The normalize lesson explains safe, step-by-step schema changes, which matter because during a rolling deploy the old and new app versions run at the same time.
add_subtopics.example: Riverside Health's ticket API needs a new status column. You run alembic revision --autogenerate, read the script, add a default value so existing rows are valid, and run alembic upgrade head in a Kubernetes Job before rolling out the new image.
add_subtopics.code:
# Alembic, run from the project folder (needs: pip install alembic)
#   alembic init migrations
#   (in migrations/env.py set target_metadata = Base.metadata, and read DATABASE_URL)
#   alembic revision --autogenerate -m "create tickets"
#   alembic upgrade head        # apply
#   alembic downgrade -1        # undo the last migration

# db.py and main.py in one file: SQLAlchemy 2.0, sync and async versions
import os
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator, Iterator

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from sqlalchemy import String, create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column, sessionmaker

# Real projects: postgresql+psycopg://user:pass@host/db  and  postgresql+asyncpg://...
DB_URL = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL", "sqlite:///demo.db")
ASYNC_URL = os.environ.get("ASYNC_DATABASE_URL", "sqlite+aiosqlite:///demo.db")

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class Ticket(Base):
    __tablename__ = "tickets"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(20), default="open")

class TicketOut(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)   # read from ORM objects
    id: int
    title: str
    status: str

class TicketIn(BaseModel):
    title: str

# --- sync version: use with plain "def" endpoints ---
engine = create_engine(DB_URL, pool_pre_ping=True)     # pool_pre_ping drops dead connections
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, expire_on_commit=False)

def get_db() -> Iterator[Session]:
    with SessionLocal() as db:                         # closes the session for us
        yield db

# --- async version: use with "async def" endpoints ---
async_engine = create_async_engine(ASYNC_URL)
AsyncSessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(async_engine, expire_on_commit=False)

async def get_async_db() -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]:
    async with AsyncSessionLocal() as session:
        yield session

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/tickets", response_model=TicketOut, status_code=201)
def create_ticket(body: TicketIn, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    ticket = Ticket(title=body.title)
    db.add(ticket)
    db.commit()                    # nothing is saved until you commit
    return ticket

@app.get("/tickets/{ticket_id}", response_model=TicketOut)
async def read_ticket(ticket_id: int, db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_async_db)):
    result = await db.execute(select(Ticket).where(Ticket.id == ticket_id))
    ticket = result.scalar_one_or_none()
    if ticket is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Ticket not found")
    return ticket

if __name__ == "__main__":
    Base.metadata.create_all(engine)       # fine for a demo; real projects use Alembic

replace_subtopics.title: Your first endpoint
replace_subtopics.body:
An endpoint is a combination of an HTTP method (GET to read, POST to create or submit, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove) and a path such as /orders/{order_id}.

In FastAPI you create an app object, then decorate a function with the method and path. Parts of the path in curly braces become path parameters. Function arguments that are not in the path become query parameters, the key=value pairs after a question mark in a URL.

Type hints do real work here. If you declare order_id: int and a client sends /orders/abc, FastAPI returns a 422 error saying the value is not a valid integer. You run the app with Uvicorn, an ASGI server (ASGI is the standard interface between Python async web apps and servers).

--reload is for development only. It watches your files and restarts the server, which costs memory and can restart at bad moments. In production run without it. A single uvicorn process uses one CPU core, so to use more cores either start several worker processes (uvicorn --workers 4, or gunicorn with the uvicorn worker class) or, on Kubernetes, run one worker per container and let replicas give you the scaling. Add --proxy-headers when the app sits behind a load balancer or ingress, so request.client and redirect URLs use the real client address and https scheme from the X-Forwarded-* headers. Add --forwarded-allow-ips with the proxy's address so only that proxy is trusted.
replace_subtopics.example: A logistics company, Crestline Freight, wants a quick way to look up shipments. GET /shipments/7731?include_events=true returns the shipment and its tracking events. GET /shipments/hello returns a 422 before any database is touched.

replace_subtopics.title: Dependencies for auth and database sessions
replace_subtopics.body:
Many endpoints need the same setup: check the caller's token, open a database connection, load settings. FastAPI handles this with dependencies. You write a function and ask for it with Depends(). FastAPI calls it before your endpoint and passes in the result.

A dependency can use yield. Code before yield runs before the request, code after yield runs after the response, which is perfect for opening and closing a database session.

If a dependency raises HTTPException(401), the endpoint never runs. You can attach a dependency to a whole router so every route is protected without repeating yourself.

The example below defines SessionLocal, the session factory, so it runs on its own. The database lesson later in this topic explains each piece. Notice that the endpoint returns a plain dictionary and raises 404 when the row is missing; returning None would send a confusing empty 200 response.
replace_subtopics.example: A bank's internal tool requires an API key in the X-API-Key header. The require_key dependency checks it against a set loaded from the environment. Requests without it get 401. Every route under /v1 is protected by one line on the router.
replace_subtopics.code:
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, sessionmaker

VALID_KEYS = {"dev-key"}

# Minimal database setup so this file runs on its own (the database
# lesson below explains it properly)
engine = create_engine("sqlite:///demo.db")
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class Account(Base):
    __tablename__ = "accounts"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100))

Base.metadata.create_all(engine)

def require_key(x_api_key: str = Header(...)):      # reads X-API-Key header
    if x_api_key not in VALID_KEYS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid API key")
    return x_api_key

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db                 # the endpoint runs while we are paused here
    finally:
        db.close()               # always runs after the response

router = APIRouter(prefix="/v1", dependencies=[Depends(require_key)])

@router.get("/accounts/{account_id}")
def get_account(account_id: int, db=Depends(get_db)):
    acct = db.get(Account, account_id)
    if acct is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Account not found")
    return {"id": acct.id, "name": acct.name}

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(router)

replace_subtopics.title: Streaming LLM answers
replace_subtopics.body:
A language model can take 10 to 30 seconds to write a long answer. If the API waits for the whole answer, users stare at a spinner. Streaming sends pieces of text to the client as soon as the model produces them.

In FastAPI you return a StreamingResponse wrapping an async generator, a function that uses yield to hand out chunks one at a time. The Anthropic Python SDK offers messages.stream(), which gives you a text_stream you can iterate over.

Server-sent events (SSE) is a simple format for streaming text over HTTP that browsers understand natively. Each chunk is a line starting with data: followed by a blank line.

Three problems appear once real users arrive. First, users close the tab. If your generator keeps running, you keep paying for tokens nobody reads. Check await request.is_disconnected() inside the loop and stop when it is true. Second, errors in the middle of a stream. The 200 status and headers were already sent, so you cannot change the status code. Catch the exception and send an error event in the stream, such as data: {"error": "..."}, and have the front end show it. Otherwise the user sees a connection that just breaks. Third, buffering. Proxies and ingress controllers, such as NGINX, often collect the response and send it in large pieces, which destroys the streaming effect. Send the header X-Accel-Buffering: no, set Cache-Control: no-cache, disable proxy buffering on the ingress, and raise idle timeouts (the default 60 seconds cuts slow answers). Sending a comment line such as ": ping" every 15 seconds keeps idle connections alive. The entnetwork lesson shows how to diagnose this when the customer's proxy is the culprit.
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital's discharge-summary assistant writes about 600 words. Without streaming, nurses wait around 20 seconds. With streaming, the first words appear in under a second and the rest arrive as they are generated, which makes the tool feel usable on a busy ward.
replace_subtopics.code:
import json
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()
llm = AsyncAnthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "MODEL"                 # placeholder model name

class Prompt(BaseModel):
    question: str

def sse(payload: dict) -> str:
    return f"data: {json.dumps(payload)}\n\n"          # SSE format

@app.post("/ask/stream")
async def ask_stream(body: Prompt, request: Request):
    async def events():
        try:
            async with llm.messages.stream(
                model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body.question}],
            ) as stream:
                async for text in stream.text_stream:          # chunks as they arrive
                    if await request.is_disconnected():        # user closed the tab
                        return                                 # stop paying for tokens
                    yield sse({"text": text})
            yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
        except Exception:
            # Headers are already sent, so we cannot change the status code.
            # Send an error event the front end can show instead.
            yield sse({"error": "The answer was interrupted. Please try again."})
    return StreamingResponse(
        events(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache",
                 "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"},   # tells NGINX not to buffer this response
    )

replace_subtopics.title: Testing with TestClient and overrides
replace_subtopics.body:
FastAPI ships a TestClient that calls your app in memory, without starting a server. You write normal pytest functions that send requests and check status codes and JSON.

The most useful testing feature is app.dependency_overrides. It lets you swap a real dependency, such as the auth check or the database session, for a fake one during tests. You can test your endpoint logic without real credentials or a real database.

Good tests for an API cover the happy path, a validation failure (422), an auth failure (401) and a not-found case (404). These are the cases a customer's integration team will hit first.

Note that the auth override alone is not enough when the endpoint also uses get_db. Without a second override, the test would open a real database session and fail, or worse, write to a real database. The example below overrides both, using a small fake class that has the same get method the endpoint calls. Always clear dependency_overrides in a finally block or a fixture, so one test cannot leak into the next.
replace_subtopics.example: Before handing the bank's API to their team, you write four tests. One checks that a valid key and account returns 200. One checks that a missing header gives 422 (the header is required). One checks that a wrong key gives 401. One overrides the database with a fake that returns nothing and checks for 404.
replace_subtopics.code:
# test_api.py   run with:  pytest -q
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app, get_db, require_key

client = TestClient(app)

class FakeAccount:
    id = 1
    name = "Test Co"

class FakeDB:
    def get(self, model, key):                    # same method the endpoint calls
        return FakeAccount() if key == 1 else None

def test_rejects_bad_key():
    r = client.get("/v1/accounts/1", headers={"X-API-Key": "nope"})
    assert r.status_code == 401

def test_missing_header_is_422():
    r = client.get("/v1/accounts/1")
    assert r.status_code == 422

def test_with_auth_and_db_overridden():
    app.dependency_overrides[require_key] = lambda: "test-key"   # skip real auth
    app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: FakeDB()          # no real database
    try:
        assert client.get("/v1/accounts/1").json() == {"id": 1, "name": "Test Co"}
        assert client.get("/v1/accounts/2").status_code == 404
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.clear()                         # always clean up

add_subtopics.title: Local multi-container dev with Docker Compose
add_subtopics.body:
A real AI service is rarely one container. The API needs a database, often a vector database, and sometimes a queue. Docker Compose describes all of them in one file, compose.yaml, and starts them together with docker compose up. It is the usual way to hand a customer a pilot that runs on any laptop or VM with Docker, and it is far easier than asking someone to install Postgres by hand.

Each entry under services is one container. Compose puts them on a private network where every service is reachable by its name, so the API connects to db and vectors, not to localhost. Use ports to expose only what a person outside needs, here just the API.

depends_on with condition: service_healthy makes the API wait until the database passes its healthcheck. A plain depends_on only waits for the container to start, and a database can take several seconds more before it accepts connections, so the API would crash at startup. Volumes keep data when containers are replaced. Without the pgdata volume, docker compose down would delete your database contents.

Keep secrets in a .env file next to compose.yaml. Compose reads it automatically to fill ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}, and env_file passes variables into the container. Add .env to .gitignore and commit an .env.example with fake values instead.

Compose is for development, demos and small single-machine pilots. It does not heal itself across machines, scale by metric or roll out safely the way Kubernetes does. Treat it as the step before Kubernetes, not a replacement for it. Useful commands: docker compose logs -f api, docker compose ps, docker compose down (keep data), docker compose down -v (delete data too).
add_subtopics.example: You bring a pilot to Crestline Freight's operations team. They have no Kubernetes yet, only a Linux VM. You give them a repository with a Dockerfile, compose.yaml and .env.example. They copy .env.example to .env, set a password and run docker compose up -d. Twenty minutes later the API, database and vector store are running.
add_subtopics.code:
# compose.yaml   start with: docker compose up --build
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    env_file: .env                     # secrets stay out of this file
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql+psycopg://app:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/app
      QDRANT_URL: http://vectors:6333  # other services are reached by name
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy     # wait until Postgres accepts connections
      vectors:
        condition: service_started
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data   # data survives container restarts
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
  vectors:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:v1.12.0
    volumes:
      - qdrant_data:/qdrant/storage
volumes:
  pgdata:
  qdrant_data:

add_subtopics.title: Jobs, CronJobs and namespaces
add_subtopics.body:
A Deployment runs things that should stay up forever. Many tasks should instead run, finish and stop: a nightly data pipeline, a database migration, a one-time backfill. Kubernetes has two objects for this. A Job runs a pod until it succeeds, and retries on failure up to backoffLimit. A CronJob creates a Job on a schedule written in cron format (five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week). Job pods must use restartPolicy Never or OnFailure, not Always.

Useful settings on a CronJob: concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, so a slow run is not overlapped by the next one; timeZone, because the default is the time zone of the cluster controller, which is often UTC; the history limits, which keep only a few finished Jobs so old pods do not pile up; and activeDeadlineSeconds on the Job, which stops a run that hangs. To test without waiting for 2 a.m., create a Job from the CronJob: kubectl create job manual-1 --from=cronjob/nightly-ingest.

Namespaces are folders inside one cluster. Customers often have claims-staging and claims-prod, or one per team. Most kubectl commands act on the default namespace unless you add -n NAME, which is a classic reason for 'my pod is missing'. A kubectl context bundles a cluster, a user and a default namespace; kubectl config get-contexts lists them, and kubectl config use-context switches. Always check kubectl config current-context before you delete or apply anything, because the wrong context means the wrong customer environment.

To reach a Service without setting up an Ingress, use kubectl port-forward. It tunnels a local port to a pod or Service through your kubectl credentials, which is ideal for debugging and for looking at an internal dashboard. It is a debugging tool, not a way to serve users.
add_subtopics.example: Riverside Health needs the schema changed before the new API version starts. You run the migration as a Job in the staging namespace, wait for it with kubectl wait --for=condition=complete, read its logs, and only then update the Deployment's image. The nightly ingest runs as a CronJob at 02:00 London time and never overlaps itself.
add_subtopics.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: {name: claims-staging}
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: {name: nightly-ingest, namespace: claims-staging}
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"            # 02:00 every day (minute hour day month weekday)
  timeZone: "Europe/London"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid        # skip a run if last night's is still going
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2              # retry a failed pod twice
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600  # kill the job after one hour
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never     # Jobs need Never or OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: ingest
              image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.2
              command: ["python", "-m", "pipeline.ingest"]
              envFrom:
                - secretRef: {name: claims-secrets}
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job                          # one-off: run database migrations
metadata: {name: migrate-1-4-2, namespace: claims-staging}
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0                  # do not retry a half-applied migration blindly
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.2
          command: ["alembic", "upgrade", "head"]
          envFrom:
            - secretRef: {name: claims-secrets}

# Everyday commands
# kubectl config get-contexts
# kubectl config use-context riverside-staging
# kubectl -n claims-staging get cronjob,job,pods
# kubectl -n claims-staging create job manual-1 --from=cronjob/nightly-ingest
# kubectl -n claims-staging wait --for=condition=complete job/migrate-1-4-2 --timeout=300s
# kubectl -n claims-staging logs job/migrate-1-4-2
# kubectl -n claims-staging port-forward service/claims-api 8080:80   # then open http://localhost:8080

replace_subtopics.title: Writing a small, safe Dockerfile
replace_subtopics.body:
A good Dockerfile starts from a slim base image, copies the dependency list before the application code (so the slow install step stays cached), and runs as a non-root user.

A multi-stage build uses two or more FROM lines. The first stage has compilers and build tools and produces the finished dependencies. The final stage copies only those results into a clean, small image. Smaller images download faster, start faster and give attackers fewer tools to use.

Never copy secrets such as .env files or API keys into an image. Anyone who can pull the image can read them. Add a .dockerignore file to keep them and other clutter out.

Four more habits prevent day-one trouble. First, CPU architecture. A new Apple Silicon Mac builds arm64 images by default, but most customer clusters run amd64 machines, and the pod fails with exec format error. Build for the target with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64. Second, set ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1. Without it Python buffers its output, and kubectl logs shows lines late or not at all. Third, pin your base image. A tag like python:3.12-slim moves when new patches are published; a digest (python:3.12-slim@sha256:...) is exact, so the same Dockerfile gives the same image next month. Fourth, scan the image for known vulnerabilities with a tool such as trivy, or with the scanner built into the customer's registry, before you push. Security teams will ask for the report.
replace_subtopics.example: Your first image for Crestline Freight was 1.9 GB because it included build tools and the test data folder. With a multi-stage build and a .dockerignore it drops to a few hundred megabytes, and a code-only change rebuilds in seconds because the dependency layer is cached.
replace_subtopics.code:
# ---- stage 1: build dependencies ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install --upgrade pip
COPY requirements.txt .
# Install into a separate folder we can copy later
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ---- stage 2: small runtime image ----
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local          # only the installed packages
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser                                   # do not run as root
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# Add near the top of the runtime stage:
#   ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
# Pin the base by digest (look it up with: docker buildx imagetools inspect python:3.12-slim):
#   FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest-you-looked-up>

# Build for the customer's amd64 cluster, even from an arm64 laptop
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 -t claims-api:1.4.2 --load .

# Check the architecture and scan for known vulnerabilities
docker image inspect claims-api:1.4.2 --format '{{.Architecture}}'   # amd64
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL claims-api:1.4.2

replace_subtopics.title: Health probes, resources and autoscaling
replace_subtopics.body:
Kubernetes needs to know whether each pod is healthy. A readiness probe answers 'can this pod take traffic right now?'. Until it passes, the Service sends it nothing, which matters when your app spends 40 seconds loading a model. A liveness probe answers 'is this pod stuck?'. If it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes restarts the container.

Resource requests tell the scheduler how much CPU and memory a pod needs so it lands on a node with room. Limits cap how much it may use. A pod that exceeds its memory limit is killed, which shows up as OOMKilled.

A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) adds or removes replicas based on a metric such as average CPU use. This lets a service handle a Monday-morning spike without paying for peak capacity all week.

Two refinements make probes safe. Use two endpoints. /live only says the process is running and should never call other systems, so a database outage does not make Kubernetes restart every healthy pod. /ready checks what the app needs to serve traffic, such as the database and the loaded model, and a failure only takes the pod out of the Service.

Slow starts are the usual cause of CrashLoopBackOff for AI apps. If a pod needs two minutes to load a model and the liveness probe starts checking after 20 seconds, Kubernetes kills the pod before it is ready, forever. A startupProbe fixes this: liveness and readiness checks wait until the startup probe passes, and the startup probe allows failureThreshold times periodSeconds of patience.

Self-hosted models need GPUs. Ask for them in resources.limits as nvidia.com/gpu: 1. GPUs are whole units, and pods cannot share one this way. Add a nodeSelector and a toleration so the pod lands on GPU nodes, which are usually tainted to keep ordinary pods away. The cluster needs the NVIDIA device plugin installed, and an unschedulable pod will say Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu in kubectl describe. The serving lesson covers model servers in more detail.
replace_subtopics.example: Crestline's tracking API averages 30 percent CPU but hits 90 percent every weekday at 9 a.m. With an HPA targeting 60 percent CPU between 3 and 10 replicas, it grows to about 7 pods during the rush and shrinks back to 3 by noon.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Inside the Deployment's container spec
startupProbe:                        # gives a slow model load time to finish
  httpGet: {path: /live, port: 8000}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 60               # 60 x 5s = up to 5 minutes to start
readinessProbe:                      # "may I send traffic?"  (checks the database too)
  httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8000}
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:                       # "am I stuck?"  (checks only the process)
  httpGet: {path: /live, port: 8000}
  periodSeconds: 20
  failureThreshold: 3
resources:
  requests: {cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi"}   # 250m = a quarter of a CPU core
  limits:   {memory: "1Gi"}
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: tracking-api}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: tracking-api}
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60}}
---
# Self-hosted model on a GPU node (needs the NVIDIA device plugin on the cluster)
# spec.template.spec:
#   nodeSelector: {gpu: "true"}                 # label the customer gives their GPU nodes
#   tolerations:
#     - {key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}
#   containers:
#     - name: llm
#       resources:
#         limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}           # whole GPUs only, set in limits

replace_subtopics.title: Ingress, rollouts and rollbacks
replace_subtopics.body:
A Service is reachable inside the cluster. To accept traffic from outside, you usually add an Ingress: a set of HTTP routing rules (hostnames, paths, TLS certificates) handled by an ingress controller such as NGINX or a cloud load balancer. Newer clusters may use the Gateway API instead, which serves the same purpose with more features.

To release a new version you change the image tag in the Deployment. By default Kubernetes performs a rolling update: it starts new pods, waits for their readiness probes, then removes old ones, so users see no downtime.

If the new version is broken, kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous version in one command. Database schema changes must be backward compatible, because old and new pods run side by side during the rollout.

A rolling update stops old pods while users may still be in the middle of requests. Kubernetes sends each stopping pod a SIGTERM signal, waits up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 by default), then kills it with SIGKILL. Your app must handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new requests, finish the in-flight ones, then exit. Uvicorn does this by default, and --timeout-graceful-shutdown sets a limit. If answers can take 60 seconds, raise the grace period above that. A short preStop sleep (5 seconds) gives the load balancer time to stop sending new requests before shutdown starts.

A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) protects you from planned disruptions, such as the customer's team draining a node for maintenance. It says how many pods must stay available, for example minAvailable: 2, so the cluster will not evict too many at once. It does not help with crashes.

If a migration changed the database, rolling back the image is not enough. The old code must still work with the new schema, which is why migrations should be backward compatible (see the normalize lesson).
replace_subtopics.example: You release claims-api 1.4.3 at 14:00. At 14:06 error rates climb because a new field is missing in production data. You run kubectl rollout undo and by 14:08 all pods are back on 1.4.2. You then fix the bug, add a test and release 1.4.4 the next morning.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Release a new version by changing the image tag
kubectl set image deployment/claims-api \
  api=123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.3

# Watch the rolling update progress
kubectl rollout status deployment/claims-api

# Something is wrong: inspect, then roll back
kubectl get pods -l app=claims-api
kubectl logs deployment/claims-api --since=10m
kubectl rollout undo deployment/claims-api

# See the revision history
kubectl rollout history deployment/claims-api

# Deployment pod spec: shut down politely
#   terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90
#   containers:
#     - name: api
#       lifecycle:
#         preStop:
#           exec: {command: ["sleep", "5"]}    # let the load balancer drain first
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: {name: claims-api}
spec:
  minAvailable: 2                # keep at least 2 pods during node maintenance
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: claims-api}

add_glossary: Docker Compose
A tool that starts several containers together from one compose.yaml file, mainly for development and small pilots.
Job
A Kubernetes object that runs a pod until it finishes successfully, then stops.
CronJob
A Kubernetes object that creates a Job on a repeating schedule.
Namespace
A named group of resources inside one cluster, used to separate teams or environments.
kubectl context
A saved combination of cluster, user and default namespace that kubectl uses.
port-forward
A kubectl command that tunnels a local port to a pod or Service, used for debugging.
Startup probe
A check that gives a slow-starting container time to become ready before liveness checks begin.
buildx
A Docker build tool that can create images for other CPU architectures, such as linux/amd64.
SIGTERM
The signal a process receives when it is asked to shut down politely.
PodDisruptionBudget
A rule that limits how many pods of an app may be down during planned maintenance.
add_practice: Write a compose.yaml with your API, Postgres (with a healthcheck and a volume) and one more service, then run docker compose up. Stop with down and start again to prove the data survived. Deliverable: the file and the output of docker compose ps.

On kind or minikube, create a namespace, run a CronJob every minute that prints the date, watch three runs, then create a Job from it manually. Deliverable: kubectl get jobs output and one sentence about what concurrencyPolicy: Forbid does.

Add startup, live and ready probes and a PodDisruptionBudget to your Deployment. Make /ready fail on purpose and show the pod leaves the Service without restarting. Deliverable: kubectl describe output and a short explanation.

add_subtopics.title: Getting access and working from the CLI
add_subtopics.body:
The first hour of a cloud engagement is about access, and the way you get it matters for security. The customer will not give you the root account or a permanent key. They will give you an identity in their directory, often through single sign-on, and a role with limited permissions.

Every cloud has a command line tool: aws, gcloud and az. All three follow the same idea. You log in once through a browser, the tool stores a short-lived token, and later commands use it. Short-lived means it expires after hours, so a leaked laptop or a copy of your config file is far less dangerous than a leaked long-lived access key. Avoid creating long-lived access keys. They end up in Git, in chat messages and in screenshots. If a script needs access, ask for a role it can assume, or for workload identity, where a service running in the cloud gets its identity from the platform with no key at all.

AWS uses named profiles, a section in ~/.aws/config for each account and role. Many customers use a separate account per environment, and you reach some accounts by assuming a role: you log in to one account and ask for temporary credentials for a role in another. A cross-account role often requires an external ID, a shared value that stops another party from tricking a service into using the role. On Google Cloud, gcloud auth login authorises the command, but your Python code needs application-default credentials, set up separately. On Azure, one login can see several subscriptions, and az account set chooses the active one.

Before running anything that changes resources, run the identity command (aws sts get-caller-identity, gcloud config list, az account show). Working in the wrong account or subscription is a common and expensive mistake. If you are behind a corporate proxy, see the entnetwork lesson for the environment variables the CLI needs.
add_subtopics.example: Riverside Health gives you SSO access to a dev account and asks you to work in a separate audit account. You log in with aws sso login, run get-caller-identity and see the dev account number. You then use the customer-audit profile, which assumes the VendorReadOnly role with the external ID they sent. You never see or store an access key.
add_subtopics.code:
# ---- AWS: single sign-on, the usual customer setup ----
aws configure sso                        # asks for the SSO start URL and region, then lets you pick account and role
aws sso login --profile customer-dev     # opens a browser; the login lasts a few hours
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile customer-dev   # WHO am I, in WHICH account? Always check first
export AWS_PROFILE=customer-dev          # so later commands use this profile

# ~/.aws/config: assume a role the customer created for you in another account
# [profile customer-audit]
# role_arn       = arn:aws:iam::210987654321:role/VendorReadOnly
# source_profile = customer-dev
# external_id    = vendor-7f3a91          # a shared secret the customer gave you

# ---- Google Cloud ----
gcloud auth login                        # for the gcloud command itself
gcloud auth application-default login    # for your Python code (Application Default Credentials)
gcloud config set project riverside-ai-dev
gcloud config list                       # confirm account and project

# ---- Azure ----
az login                                 # add --use-device-code on a machine with no browser
az account list --output table           # every subscription you can see
az account set --subscription "Riverside Dev"
az account show                          # confirm the active subscription

az login, read by the Azure SDK

add_subtopics.title: Choosing where code runs
add_subtopics.body:
Every cloud offers several ways to run your API or model, and the right choice depends on the workload and on the customer's people. There are four main families.

Virtual machines (EC2, Compute Engine, Azure Virtual Machines) give you a whole Linux server. You control everything and pay for it while it runs, but you also patch it, secure it and scale it. They suit GPU boxes for self-hosted models and legacy software.

Managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) runs containers on a cluster the cloud helps to operate. It is powerful and portable, and many enterprises already run it, but it needs people who know Kubernetes.

Serverless containers (Cloud Run, ECS on Fargate, Azure Container Apps) run your container image without you managing servers. They can scale to zero when idle and often need no cluster knowledge. Limits include request time limits, few or no GPUs, and less control over networking.

Functions (Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions) run one small piece of code per event. They are great for glue: react to a file upload, run a short job. They are a poor fit for long jobs and for large model files.

A cold start is the delay when a platform has to start a new instance after idle time. It can add seconds, which is fine for a nightly job and painful for a chat screen. Keeping one instance warm removes it, at a cost. Cost also differs: pay-per-use is cheap for spiky, light traffic, while steady, heavy traffic is usually cheaper on always-on machines.

Finally, ask who will operate it after you leave. A serverless container that the customer's two-person team can understand often beats a perfect Kubernetes design they cannot run. See the deploy lesson for the container and Kubernetes details.
add_subtopics.example: Crestline Freight wants a tracking API with light, spiky traffic and has no Kubernetes staff. You choose a serverless container service with one warm instance. Harbor Mutual wants a self-hosted model on a GPU and already runs a cluster, so you use a GPU node pool on their managed Kubernetes.
add_subtopics.code:
# Deploy the same container image to a serverless container platform
# Google Cloud Run
gcloud run deploy tracking-api \
  --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/riverside-ai-dev/apps/tracking-api:1.4.2 \
  --region europe-west1 --min-instances 1 --memory 1Gi --no-allow-unauthenticated

# Azure Container Apps
az containerapp create --name tracking-api --resource-group rg-riverside-dev \
  --environment riverside-env --image myregistry.azurecr.io/tracking-api:1.4.2 \
  --min-replicas 1 --target-port 8000 --ingress internal

# AWS: the same idea is an ECS service on Fargate (usually defined in Terraform)

replace_subtopics.title: Networking: VPCs, subnets and security groups
replace_subtopics.body:
A VPC is your own isolated network inside the cloud, defined by an IP address range written in CIDR notation, for example 10.20.0.0/16 (about 65,000 addresses). You split it into subnets, smaller ranges that live in one availability zone.

A public subnet has a route to the internet through an internet gateway. A private subnet does not. Databases and model servers belong in private subnets so nothing on the internet can reach them directly. They can still call out through a NAT gateway if the customer allows it.

A security group is a firewall attached to a resource. You list which traffic may come in, for example 'port 5432 only from the app's security group'. By default everything inbound is denied.

The example defines the api security group that the database rule refers to. Without it, terraform validate stops with a reference error. Private subnets have no route to the internet, so calls to object storage would need a NAT gateway, which costs money per hour and per gigabyte. A gateway endpoint for S3 (Google Cloud and Azure have equivalents, such as Private Google Access and service endpoints) adds a private route to the storage service instead, at no hourly cost, and keeps the traffic off the public internet.
replace_subtopics.example: For Riverside Health you create a VPC with two public subnets for the load balancer and two private subnets for the API pods and the database. The database security group allows port 5432 only from the API security group, so even a mistake elsewhere cannot expose patient records to the internet.

replace_subtopics.title: IAM and least privilege
replace_subtopics.body:
IAM controls who can do what to which resource. A policy is a document listing allowed actions (such as s3:GetObject) on specific resources (such as one bucket). A role is an identity that a service can assume to get temporary credentials, so you never store long-lived access keys in your code.

Least privilege means giving each service only the permissions it needs, and nothing more. A document search service needs to read one bucket. It does not need to delete buckets or read the finance team's data.

In Terraform, the aws_iam_policy_document data source lets you write policies in HCL instead of hand-written JSON, which is easier to read and review.

Encryption keys add one more permission to remember. Each cloud has a key service: AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS and Azure Key Vault. Banks and hospitals often require customer-managed keys (CMK), where the customer creates and controls the key and can switch off access by disabling it. The service still needs permission to use that key. A very common surprise is AccessDenied when reading an object even though s3:GetObject is allowed: if the bucket is encrypted with a KMS key (SSE-KMS), the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key, and kms:GenerateDataKey to write. Both the key policy and the IAM policy must allow it.
replace_subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual's security reviewer rejects your first draft because it grants s3:* on every bucket. You rewrite it to allow only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the claims-documents bucket. The review passes the same day.

replace_subtopics.title: The Terraform workflow and state
replace_subtopics.body:
Terraform has a short loop. terraform init downloads providers, the plugins that talk to AWS, GCP or Azure. terraform plan compares your code with what exists and prints what it would create, change or destroy. terraform apply makes those changes.

Terraform remembers what it created in a state file. The state maps each resource in your code to a real object in the cloud. For a team, state must live in a remote backend, such as an S3 bucket, with locking so two people cannot apply at the same time.

State files can contain secrets, so never commit them to git. Read every plan before applying, and look hardest at lines marked destroy or 'must be replaced', because replacing a database means losing its data.

Three more tools complete the workflow. A moved block records a rename, so Terraform updates its state instead of destroying and recreating. An import block brings a resource that someone created by hand in the console under Terraform's control. Write the block, run terraform plan, and it will show the import; then complete the resource arguments until the plan shows no changes. The older command terraform import does the same one resource at a time. Finally, drift means the real cloud no longer matches the code, because someone edited it by hand. Run terraform plan -detailed-exitcode in a scheduled CI job. Its exit code is 0 for no changes, 1 for an error and 2 when changes are needed, so a job can alert on 2.

Remote state needs locking, so two people cannot apply at once. With the S3 backend, set use_lockfile = true for S3-native locking (Terraform 1.11 and later). Older customer repositories may still use dynamodb_table, which is deprecated but works, so recognise it when you see it.
replace_subtopics.example: You change the database instance size from db.t3.medium to db.t3.large. The plan says '~ update in-place', which is safe. A colleague renames the database resource in code, and the plan says '-/+ destroy and then create replacement'. You stop, and use a moved block instead so Terraform understands it is the same database.
replace_subtopics.code:
# One-time setup: download providers, connect to the remote state backend
terraform init

# Format and check the code
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform validate

# Preview changes and save the exact plan for review
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt    # paste into the pull request

# Apply exactly the plan that was reviewed
terraform apply tfplan

# Inspect what Terraform is tracking
terraform state list

# Rename without replacing the database
moved {
  from = aws_db_instance.db
  to   = aws_db_instance.claims_db
}

# Adopt a bucket somebody created by hand
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy_reports
  id = "riverside-legacy-reports"      # the real bucket name
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "legacy_reports" {
  bucket = "riverside-legacy-reports"
}

# Remote state with S3-native locking
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "riverside-tfstate"
    key          = "claims/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    use_lockfile = true                # older repos: dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
  }
}

# In CI: detect drift (exit code 2 means the cloud differs from the code)
#   terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -input=false

replace_subtopics.title: Variables, modules and environments
replace_subtopics.body:
Hard-coded values make code hard to reuse. Terraform variables let you pass in values such as the region, instance size or environment name. Outputs expose values, such as a load balancer URL, for other code or people to use.

A module is a folder of Terraform files you can call like a function, with inputs and outputs. You might write one 'ai_service' module that creates the network rules, role and database for a service, then call it once for staging and once for production with different sizes.

Keep each environment's state separate, for example in a different backend key or a different cloud account, so a mistake in staging cannot touch production.

Four more features you will meet in customer repositories. count and for_each create several similar resources from one block: count for a number, for_each for a set or map, which is safer because each item is tracked by its key instead of its position. Data sources look up things that already exist, such as the VPC and subnets the customer's network team built, so you use their network instead of creating a new one. Pin your provider versions in required_providers, so a new provider release cannot change your plan overnight; commit the generated .terraform.lock.hcl file. Some customers require OpenTofu, the open-source fork of Terraform managed by the Linux Foundation. The commands are the same, with tofu instead of terraform, and most simple configurations work in both.

You call the same module twice: staging with a small database and 2 replicas, production with a larger database, 3 replicas and deletion protection on. The two stacks stay identical in shape, so what worked in staging is what ships.

replace_subtopics.title: Corporate proxies and HTTPS_PROXY
replace_subtopics.body:
Most command-line tools and libraries look for proxy settings in environment variables. HTTPS_PROXY is the proxy for https URLs, HTTP_PROXY for http URLs, and NO_PROXY lists hosts that must be reached directly. Tools differ on case: curl only reads lowercase http_proxy for http URLs, so set both cases to be safe. The proxy URL itself usually starts with http://, even for HTTPS traffic, because the request to the proxy is a plain CONNECT.

NO_PROXY matters as much as the proxy. Internal services, the metadata service on cloud machines and localhost should bypass the proxy, or requests to them fail. Support for wildcards and IP ranges in NO_PROXY varies by tool, so test each one.

A 407 Proxy Authentication Required status means the proxy wants credentials. Service accounts can often put a user and password in the proxy URL (URL-encode special characters). Some proxies use Windows login protocols such as NTLM or Kerberos, which many tools do not support; a local helper proxy or an allowlist exception for your server is the usual fix. Some tools, such as git, npm, pip and the Docker daemon, also keep their own proxy settings.

Containers and clusters need their own proxy settings, because they do not inherit the shell variables of your laptop. There are three separate places. The Docker daemon, which pulls images, runs as a system service and needs the variables in a systemd drop-in file (or in daemon.json for newer versions); exporting HTTPS_PROXY in your terminal does nothing for docker pull. docker build runs commands such as pip install inside temporary containers, so pass --build-arg HTTPS_PROXY=... (Docker accepts proxy build arguments without an ARG line in the Dockerfile). Running containers get variables with -e or env in compose. In Kubernetes, set the variables in the pod's env in the Deployment. Always include in NO_PROXY the names the cluster uses internally: .svc, .cluster.local, and the cluster and service address ranges (for example 10.96.0.0/12), or your pods will try to reach each other through the corporate proxy and fail.

Often the best answer is not a proxy at all. When pypi.org, npmjs.org or Docker Hub are blocked, security teams usually run an internal package mirror such as Artifactory or Nexus that caches approved packages. You point your tools at it: pip's index-url, npm's registry and Docker's registry-mirrors setting. Ask IT for the mirror URLs on day one, and for a service account token if the mirror needs login.
replace_subtopics.example: At Garnetvale, pip install works but the app's calls to an internal document service time out. env shows HTTPS_PROXY is set and NO_PROXY is empty, so internal calls go to the proxy, which cannot route back inside. Adding .garnetvale.internal and 10.0.0.0/8 to NO_PROXY fixes it in a minute.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Most tools read these variables (curl reads lowercase http_proxy only)
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080
export HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,.garnetvale.internal,10.0.0.0/8
export https_proxy=$HTTPS_PROXY http_proxy=$HTTP_PROXY no_proxy=$NO_PROXY

# Proxy that needs a login: URL-encode special characters in the password
export HTTPS_PROXY="http://svc-ai:P%40ss%21word@proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080"

# Some tools keep their own settings
git config --global http.proxy http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080
npm config set https-proxy http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080
pip config set global.proxy http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080

# Quick checks
env | grep -i proxy                       # what does this shell actually have?
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://api.vendor.example/v1/health

# Docker daemon: give the SERVICE its own proxy (needed for docker pull)
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf <<'EOF'
[Service]
Environment="HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080"
Environment="NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,.garnetvale.internal"
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart docker
docker info | grep -i proxy               # confirm the daemon picked it up

# docker build: commands inside the build need the proxy too
docker build --build-arg HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080 \
             --build-arg NO_PROXY=localhost,.garnetvale.internal -t claims-api:1.4.2 .

# Kubernetes: in the Deployment's container spec
#   env:
#     - {name: HTTPS_PROXY, value: "http://proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080"}
#     - {name: NO_PROXY,    value: "localhost,127.0.0.1,.svc,.cluster.local,10.96.0.0/12,.garnetvale.internal"}

# Internal package mirrors (Artifactory or Nexus) instead of the public internet
pip config set global.index-url https://artifactory.garnetvale.internal/artifactory/api/pypi/pypi-remote/simple
npm config set registry https://artifactory.garnetvale.internal/artifactory/api/npm/npm-remote/
# Docker: /etc/docker/daemon.json  ->  {"registry-mirrors": ["https://registry-mirror.garnetvale.internal"]}

replace_subtopics.title: TLS inspection and custom CA bundles
replace_subtopics.body:
TLS certificates are trusted because a certificate authority signed them and your software has a list of trusted CAs, called a trust store or CA bundle. Under TLS inspection, the certificate you receive is signed by the company's inspection CA. If your program does not trust that CA, you see errors such as CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED or 'self-signed certificate in certificate chain'.

Different runtimes use different trust stores. Browsers and curl usually use the operating system's store, which IT already updated. Python's requests uses the certifi bundle shipped with the library. Java has its own cacerts keystore. Node.js has a built-in list. So the browser working proves little.

The fix is to get the corporate root CA as a PEM file, build a bundle containing the public CAs plus that root, and point each runtime at it. Some variables replace the default list (REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE), while NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS adds to it, which is why you combine files first. For Python 3.10 and later, the truststore package makes Python use the operating system's store instead. Never turn verification off; it removes protection and will fail a security review.

Java needs its own step because it ignores every variable above. Its trust store is a file called cacerts, and you add the corporate root with the keytool command. The file lives under the JDK folder (lib/security/cacerts in Java 9 and later, jre/lib/security/cacerts in Java 8), and the default password is changeit. Changing the JDK's own file is lost when Java is upgraded, so many teams instead create a separate truststore file and point Java at it with -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore. Remember that a custom truststore replaces the default one, so copy cacerts first and add to the copy.

Containers do not see the host's certificates. Inside an image, copy the root CA into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ (the file name must end in .crt) and run update-ca-certificates in the Dockerfile. That updates the image's system store, which OpenSSL, curl and most tools then trust. Python requests still uses certifi, so also set REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE to the system bundle, and give Node the file with NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS.
replace_subtopics.example: Garnetvale's AI service fails with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED when calling the model provider, while the browser on the same server works. openssl shows the issuer is Garnetvale Inspection CA. The FDE gets the root CA from the security team, bakes a combined bundle into the container image and sets REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and SSL_CERT_FILE. The calls succeed with verification fully on.
replace_subtopics.code:
# 1. See who signed the certificate you actually receive
openssl s_client -connect api.vendor.example:443 -servername api.vendor.example \
    -proxy proxy.garnetvale.internal:8080 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject
# issuer=CN = Garnetvale Inspection CA   <- their proxy, not a public CA

# 2. Get the corporate root CA as a PEM file from IT (or export it from the OS store)
# 3. Build one bundle = public CAs + corporate root, and point each runtime at it
cat "$(python -m certifi)" garnetvale-root-ca.pem > ca-bundle.pem
export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=$PWD/ca-bundle.pem          # Python requests
export SSL_CERT_FILE=$PWD/ca-bundle.pem               # OpenSSL-based tools, many others
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=$PWD/garnetvale-root-ca.pem  # Node adds this to its list
export AWS_CA_BUNDLE=$PWD/ca-bundle.pem               # AWS CLI and boto3
git config --global http.sslCAInfo $PWD/ca-bundle.pem
pip config set global.cert $PWD/ca-bundle.pem

# Alternative for Python 3.10+: use the operating system's trust store
#   pip install truststore
#   import truststore; truststore.inject_into_ssl()

# Java: add the corporate root to the JDK's own trust store
keytool -importcert -alias garnetvale-root -file garnetvale-root-ca.pem \
        -keystore "$JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts" -storepass changeit -noprompt

# Or, keep a separate copy and point one program at it
cp "$JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts" my-truststore.jks
keytool -importcert -alias garnetvale-root -file garnetvale-root-ca.pem \
        -keystore my-truststore.jks -storepass changeit -noprompt
java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=$PWD/my-truststore.jks \
     -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit -jar app.jar

# Dockerfile: make every runtime in the image trust the corporate CA
#   COPY garnetvale-root-ca.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/garnetvale-root-ca.crt
#   RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates \
#       && update-ca-certificates
#   ENV REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt \
#       NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/garnetvale-root-ca.crt

replace_subtopics.title: Firewalls, allowlists and egress rules
replace_subtopics.body:
Egress means outbound traffic, from the customer's network out; ingress means inbound. Security teams in regulated industries usually deny all egress by default and allow only listed destinations, often only through the proxy. Getting on that allowlist is a change request that may need approval from a change board, so ask early.

A good request is specific. List source machines or subnets, destination hostnames, ports, protocol, direction, whether traffic goes through the proxy, what data is sent, expected volume and a named owner. Prefer fully qualified hostnames over IP addresses, because cloud APIs sit behind content delivery networks whose IPs change. If the vendor publishes IP ranges, include the link.

Ingress is harder than egress. If a vendor needs to call the customer, for example with webhooks, that needs an inbound rule, a public endpoint and usually a security review. Where possible, design so the customer's side calls out and pulls data, which only needs egress.

Also ask whether some domains are exempt from TLS inspection. Tools that pin certificates break under inspection and need an exception.

The allowlist can also work in the other direction. Some vendor APIs, and many banks' own systems, only accept calls from known addresses. Then the customer must tell the vendor which public IP addresses their traffic leaves from, which are usually the addresses of the proxy or NAT gateway, and the vendor adds them to its own allowlist. Ask the customer's network team for these addresses early, because a change on the vendor side can take days. Ask whether the addresses are fixed and whether there is more than one, such as a second data centre for failover.

Some enterprise APIs also require mutual TLS (mTLS). In normal TLS only the server proves who it is. In mTLS your client also presents a certificate, issued by the customer or the vendor, so the server knows exactly which system is calling. You need the client certificate and its private key, and you must keep the key secret. If a request fails with a TLS handshake error only for this API, ask whether it needs a client certificate.

It is approved at the next weekly change board. A second team that asked for 'internet access for the AI server' waited five weeks and got a question back.

replace_subtopics.title: Diagnosing 'works on my laptop, not in their network'
replace_subtopics.body:
The internet lesson taught checking layers in order: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP. In a corporate network add three rules.

First, test from the machine that fails, and inside the container if the app runs in one. Your laptop, the server and a container can each have different proxy variables, DNS servers and trust stores.

Second, compare two clients on the same machine. If curl works and Python fails, the network is fine and the difference is in settings: a proxy variable the program does not read, or a CA bundle it does not use. If both fail the same way, take the evidence to the network team.

Third, read the error precisely. A timeout usually means a firewall dropping packets or a missing proxy. 'Connection refused' means something answered and said no. 407 is the proxy asking for a login. A 403 with an HTML block page from a security product is a URL policy, not the API. A certificate error that names the company's CA is TLS inspection. The widget above walks through this as a decision tree, and the checklist below is what to gather before you ask for help.

One symptom deserves its own note: streaming. A normal request may work perfectly, but a server-sent events or WebSocket connection dies after 30 or 60 seconds, or the answer arrives all at once at the end. The cause is usually a proxy or load balancer that buffers responses or cuts connections it thinks are idle. Check it by running curl -N (no buffering) and watching whether chunks arrive live, and note the time at which the connection drops. Then ask the network team to disable response buffering for your host and raise the idle timeout, or make your server send a small heartbeat line every 15 seconds so the connection never looks idle. WebSockets also need the proxy to allow the Upgrade header.
replace_subtopics.example: Garnetvale's batch job times out, but curl from the same server works. The script prints nothing for proxy variables, because the scheduler starts jobs with a clean environment. Adding HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY to the job definition fixes it. The whole diagnosis takes 20 minutes because the FDE ran the checks below from the scheduler itself.
replace_subtopics.code:
#!/bin/bash
# netcheck.sh HOST  -- run it FROM the machine or container that fails
HOST=$1
echo "== proxy settings";  env | grep -i -E '^(https?|no)_proxy=' || echo "none set"
echo "== DNS";             nslookup "$HOST" | tail -n 3
echo "== direct TCP 443";  nc -vz -w 5 "$HOST" 443 2>&1 | tail -n 1
echo "== via curl (uses proxy vars)"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "status=%{http_code} proxy_connect=%{http_connect}\n" \
     --max-time 15 "https://$HOST/" || echo "curl failed: see error above"
echo "== certificate issuer seen by this machine"
curl -sv --max-time 15 "https://$HOST/" -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i "issuer" | head -n 1
echo "== which CA bundle Python uses"
python3 -c "import ssl, certifi; print(ssl.get_default_verify_paths().cafile, certifi.where())"

# Streaming test: chunks should appear one by one, not all at the end
curl -N --max-time 120 -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
     -d '{"question": "Write a long answer"}' -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     https://api.vendor.example/ask/stream | while read -r line; do echo "$(date +%T) $line"; done
# Timestamps that jump together mean buffering. A stop at 30s or 60s means an idle timeout.
checklist: Run the checks on the failing machine, and inside the container if there is one
Record the exact error text and the time it happened
Note proxy variables and NO_PROXY as the program sees them
Check DNS: does the name resolve, to a public or private address?
Check TCP to port 443 directly and through the proxy
Record the certificate issuer the machine actually receives
Compare curl with your program on the same machine
Send the network team source, destination, port, time and output

add_glossary: Docker daemon proxy
The proxy setting of the Docker background service, separate from your shell, needed to pull images.
Package mirror
An internal server, such as Artifactory or Nexus, that serves approved copies of public packages and images.
keytool
The Java command for managing keystores and truststores, used to add a corporate CA.
update-ca-certificates
A Linux command that rebuilds the system trust store from certificates in /usr/local/share/ca-certificates.
mTLS
Mutual TLS: both the server and the client present certificates to prove who they are.
Static egress IP
A fixed public address that a network's outbound traffic uses, which vendors can allowlist.
Idle timeout
How long a proxy waits with no data before it cuts a connection.
